=== FILE: 6 Popular Supplements That Aren’t Worth It [n07IYWQ9Ow0].txt ===

 niki, frosting, frosting, frosting, frosting, frosting, frosting, frosting, frosting, frosting, through six popular supplements that I think aren't worth it, at least for most people. Number one, Mitopure. The most expensive supplement on this list is Mitopure, which is a patented form of Urolithin A. It costs $112 a month and is marketed as clinically proven to improve strength by 12% and other things like endurance. You might have seen my video criticizing the studies done on Mitopure. Here's a quick summary. The increased 12% strength is 12% increase in hamstring strength, not 12% increase in your leg press strength or anything like that. There's no effect on upper body strength or grip strength, no effect on VO2 peak or peak power output, and only a minor effect on the six-minute walking test, and you were able to walk only a few thousand meters further within the six minutes. Muscle endurance, as tested by a muscle contraction test, was not seen to result in improvements compared to placebo after four months. No effect on immune cells that have a big effect on age-related immune function, like T-memory stem cells, CD3, CD8, and CD4 cells, some minor effects on CD8 T-cells. Since there's no effect on T-memory stem cells, these changes would not have any significant effect on immune decline, no effect on body composition and fat loss or muscle mass, and conflicting results on inflammation markers, with some studies finding an effect and others not. So overall, we're talking about extremely small effects, and these effects are in parameters that aren't that clinically meaningful. You would get much better results from just exercise, especially when we're talking about body composition and strength effects. Even the idea of increasing mitophagy, the clearance of old mitochondria with Mitopure, you're going to increase mitophagy a lot more with exercise. Honestly, I think that AG1 has more benefits than Mitopure, but don't worry, AG1 is also on this list. I'm not going to go into the slightly suspicious and questionable research methodology done on the Mitopure studies. You can check out my other videos about it, but needless to say, these studies are a little bit suspicious. Next up, BCAAs and EAAs. When I was growing up, BCAAs were the thing. You were supposed to take BCAAs in between meals to prevent muscle loss. Clinical trials show that BCAAssupplementation has no effect on muscle growth or exercise performance. The only real benefit is reduced muscle soreness after exercise. Not only do BCAAs do nothing for muscle growth, they appear to increase protein breakdown, because the BCAAs contain only three essential amino acids, leucine, isoleucine, and valine, but you're missing six other essential amino acids that are needed for protein synthesis. So whenever you drink BCAAs, where does your body get these other six amino acids? It takes it from its own muscle tissue. The only real use case for BCAAs is adding it to a protein powder that doesn't have all the essential amino acids, let's say hemp protein or collagen protein. Excess circulating BCAAs can also block the uptake of tryptophan into the brain, which prevents the production of serotonin, the neurotransmitter of calmness and relaxation. So taking BCAAs alone either does nothing or it has actually negative effects. What about EAAs, all the nine essential amino acids? The International Society of Sports Nutrition claims that EAAs stimulate protein synthesis at rest and during exercise, and they can also improve muscle function and strength in aging populations. However, clinical trials on younger individuals have seen that EAAs alone don't increase lean mass or strength compared to placebo, but they do when combined with resistance training. EAAs are significantly better than BCAAs because they contain all the nine essential amino acids. However, EAAs are inferior to something like whey protein or any other protein powder because in addition to the essential amino acids you get from whey protein, you also get additional protein, which is going to be superior for muscle growth. So if you are going to spend money on EAAs, spend it on protein powder instead. Next up, we have all these different types of creatine. Don't get me wrong, creatine is one of the most researched supplements out there. It has research benefits and it's certainly one of the lowest hanging fruit in terms of supplementation. The issue is that companies keep releasing different types of creatine that are supposedly better than the old creatine monohydrate. Creatine HCL, creatine ethyl ester and so on. These versions are usually much more expensive and they're often marketed as solving problems that regular creatine supposedly call us. Things like digestive issues, kidney problems or hair loss. Maybe there will be a more powerful form of creatine in the few years. But right now, for most people, plain old creatine monohydrate is the best form. It's also the cheapest. Pentadecanoic acid or C15 is a saturated fatty acid found in dairy fats that's been found to have anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties in cell studies. In observational studies, higher C15 levels are associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular disease, diabetes and colorectal cancer. The reason for this is thought that C15 helps to stabilize cell membranes or it could be also something else in the dairy foods which is the main source of C15 in people's diets. Nowadays, C15 is sold under the fatty 15 supplement and unfortunately, the randomness control trials on the supplement have been quite disappointing. A 2024 trial on overweight individuals saw that taking 200 mg a day of C15 for 12 weeks increased plasma C15 levels significantly compared to placebo. Those whose plasma C15 reached over 5 micrograms per milliliter saw a statistically significant decrease in liver enzymes, ALT-29 units per liter, ASD-6 and GGT-11. They also saw a 0.6 gram per deciliter increase in hemoglobin, which is significant. However, only 50% of the people out of 20 reached plasma C15 of over 5 micrograms per milliliter, which was the effective range. Those who didn't reach that threshold didn't see improvements. The reason why half of the participants didn't reach the required threshold was that they didn't adhere to the protocol and they weren't taking the supplement as consistently. Furthermore, the participants saw no difference in cholesterol, glucose, and inflammation, probably because their levels were within normal range to begin with, whereas that wasn't the case with their liver enzymes. So C15 supplementation might only work in improving markers that are not optimal, and it might work only in some people and not others. Another 2024 randomized controlled trial saw that C15 supplementation, together with the Mediterranean-style diet, resulted in a significantly greater decrease in LDL cholesterol compared to just the diet protocol without C15. However, the addition of C15 to the diet didn't produce additional benefits on lowering total cholesterol, triglycerides, liver enzymes, insulin, and HOMA-IR. The participants had elevations in these markers at baseline, but the improvements in them were achievable already with a Mediterranean-style diet, with C15 providing no additional benefits. The diet prescribed in this trial did allow dairy, but it was low-fat dairy, and they recommended limiting other animal fats. So it's not clear if C15 would be beneficial beyond a standard Mediterranean diet, with the exception of LDL reduction. So the overall evidence suggests that people with higher circulating C15 levels do appear to have less heart disease and lower mortality. But this doesn't prove that supplementing C15 would give you the same results, or that C15 supplementation would be responsible for this reduction, because supplementing C15 doesn't appear to have any effect on cholesterol, blood sugar, inflammation, and some other markers, only liver markers in overweight people. A 2025 systematic review found that 8 out of 10 studies show no significant effect on testosterone from tribulus terrestris supplementation, and the two studies that did show a benefit showed only a small increase, around 60-70 nanograms per deciliter increase. The positive results were seen mostly in men with low baseline testosterone. The evidence for most testosterone boosters is quite weak. The ones that have strong evidence for increasing testosterone include ashwagandha, mostly in stressed or infertile men, tongat ali, mostly in stressed or hypogonadal men, zinc, only if you have low zinc status, and vitamin D, only if your vitamin D is deficient or you're obese. === FILE: Body Fat and Longevity： What The Science Actually Says [Lz2h6lszPHA].en.txt ===

We all know obesity is bad. It can cut 10 to 15 years off your life. But it's not just about how much body fat you have. It's about where you store it. Your body can store fat in many places. Under the skin, which is called subcutaneous fat, and around the organs and in between muscles, which is called visceral fat. Visceral fat is the real killer. It drives up your risk of heart disease, diabetes, and early death more than almost anything else. A new UK bioank study saw that visceral fat, intramuscular fat, and liver fat were the strongest predictors of cardiovascular aging in both men and women. The interesting thing is that the study found that subcutaneous fat, the fat under your skin, was associated with increased aging in only men, but not in women. This is a repeating pattern you see in other studies as well. In this study in Iran, there was a pretty linear relationship between body fat percentage and increased risk of mortality among men. Anything above 15% body fat was associated with a higher risk of mortality. For women, however, there was no correlation at body fat percentages between 20 and 35%. Only severe obesity over 35% body fat and below 20%, which is an indication of being underweight for women where associated with increased risk. So, when it comes to body fat under the skin, the one that you can pinch and grab, then it's not that big of a concern, especially for women. as long as the woman isn't severely obese with a body fat percentage over 35%. Now, for men, however, it's a different story. For men, being leaner is protective against heart disease and premature mortality. For men, anything above 15% body fat appears to increase the risk of mortality in a linear fashion. The higher the body fat percentage, the higher the risk is. What it means for men is that they need to keep their body fat on the leaner side. I'm not talking about being singledigit body fat, but around 10 to 12% body fat probably is the sweet spot. Here's what 10% body fat generally looks like for men. Of course, it's influenced by muscle mass. If you have more muscle, then you look leaner and more jacked, but in this photo, I'm probably around 10% body fat, maybe 9% at the lowest. Here's a photo of me around 13 to 14% body fat. And here's a photo of me around 8 to 9% body fat. However, when it comes to the visceral fat around the organs, then it's harmful for both men and women. It's probably even more harmful for men than it is for women. But both sexes want to keep their visceral fat on the lower side. Visceral fat, the fat around the organs and inside the muscles, increases with age in both men and women. In your 20s, the average visceral fat mass is around 420 g for males and 230 g for women. This increases to up to 2,000 grams in men in their 80s and 1150 grams in women in their 80s. So one of the key reasons why women die to less heart disease and they live significantly longer than men might be that they have less visceral fat. Despite having more subcutaneous fat, the higher amount of subcutaneous fat in women doesn't increase their risk of mortality. It means that visceral fat, the belly fat is really bad for your risk of heart disease and mortality. So what is the reason why women have significantly less visceral fat than men do? is estrogen. Women have 10 to 20 times more estrogen than men for the first 50 years of their life and this gives them five decades where they have a slower progression of heart disease. Estrogen also promotes fat storage around the hips as subcutaneous fat instead of visceral fat. How do you know how much visceral fat you have? The most accurate method is to take a full body MRI, but it can be more costly. The second best option is the DEXA scan. That's much cheaper, but the DEXA scan can be a little bit less accurate, although not completely wrong. For example, my recent DEXA scan showed my visceral fat was 150 grams, whereas it was 250 grams on the MRI. I took them two days apart. You can also predict your visceral fat to a certain extent by measuring your waist circumference. That's because visceral fat accumulates around the organs, especially around the belly. A 2014 study on over 650,000 people saw that waist circumference was linearly associated with an increased risk of all cause mortality in both men and women. The lowest risk was observed at 85 cm or 33.5 in in men and 65 cm or 25.5 in in women. A waist circumference of 100 cm or 39 in in men and 75 cm or 29.5 in women is still acceptable but not optimal. So you want to get your waist circumference lower because having a lower waist circumference means you have less visceral fat. All right, let me recap some of the main points. For women, subcutaneous fat under the skin isn't a big concern, as long as you're not over 35% body fat in the severe obesity category. For men, subcutaneous fat over 15% is linearly associated with a higher mortality risk. So, it's better to stay leaner as a man, around 10 to 12% body fat. For both men and women, a higher amount of visceral fat is a risk factor for heart disease and mortality. Both men and women should get their visceral fat low, at least below 450 gram for men and below 300 gram for women. Weight circumference can be a proxy measure of visceral fat, but it's not 100% reliable. For men, a healthy waist circumference is below 90 cm and for women below 75 cm. So, how do you go about losing the visceral fat? The obvious answer is to just lose body fat. If you lose subcutaneous fat by cleaning up your diet, losing some weight, and implementing exercise, you will see a reduction in visceral fat as well. Basically, if you're 30% body fat, you'll have less visceral fat if you go down to 20% body fat or 10% body fat. The higher your total body fat percentage, the higher amount of subcutaneous body fat you have, the higher your visceral fat generally tends to be. But you can still be otherwise lean around 10% body fat and still have suboptimal amounts of visceral fat. It's not going to be thousands of grams, but you can be 10% body fat and still have maybe 500 grams of visceral fat, which is not optimal. I have very low visceral fat. At the lowest, it was 54 grams. There were specific and science-based changes I made to my exercise and diet that enabled me to specifically target visceral fat. Check out my video about what I did

=== FILE: Can These Meds Really Help You Live Longer？ [sfhKnpwIiNc].en.txt ===

Scientists are constantly trying to find the next drug that would slow down aging and extend lifespan. There are several compounds and supplements that have been identified in the interventions testing program on mice. However, a recent study discovered that certain medications and pharmaceuticals might also reduce the risk of all cause mortality in the general population. I'm going to go through the drugs that were associated with increased mortality as well as decreased mortality risk. The paper was published in 2024 in the journal Aging Sill. They took data from half a million UK individuals and analyzed the effects of 406 commonly prescribed drugs on all cause mortality over a 13.8year median follow-up. What they found was that 92% of the drugs were associated with increased mortality risk, which isn't surprising. That's because pharmaceuticals are usually prescribed for people who have certain medical conditions. So, it's not the drugs that kill them, it's the disease. Here's a list of the top nine drugs that were associated with increased risk of mortality. Opioids like morphine and oramorph were associated with a 450% higher mortality risk. Fuosomide which is a diuretic with a 100% higher risk. Paracetamol which is an antipuretic with 48% higher risk. Tiotropo which is a broncoilator used to treat chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and asthma 98% higher risk. Amlipene which is a blood pressure medication with A-50% higher risk. Metaclopram which is used to treat reflux and gastric problems with a 38% increased risk. This is very interesting but we have to remember that it's an observational study. These drugs likely do not increase mortality directly, but they're associated with increased mortality because they're often prescribed in the context of a serious terminal health condition or disease. What about the drugs that were seen to be associated with decreased mortality risk? They found that out of 400 drugs, only 14 of them had mortality benefits. Here are the top nine drugs seen to reduce mortality risk. A tovastatin, which is a statin for heart disease, was associated with a 9% lower risk of mortality. Selenaphil, which is a PD5 inhibitor used to treat erectile dysfunction with a 15% lower risk. Neproxen, which is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, with a 10% lower risk. Estraderm, which is an estrogen patch, with a 33% lower risk. Vagifam, which is an estrogen tablet, with a 27% lower risk. Automise, which is an ear spray for ear infections, with a 15% lower risk. Estrial, which is an estrogen cream, with a 26% lower risk. Lime Cyclan, which is an antibiotic used to treat acne, with a 31% lower risk. And estradiol, which is an estrogen pill, with a 25% lower risk. The researchers also looked at the class of drugs and their effects on mortality. The class of drugs that was associated with the greatest reduction in mortality risk 36% reduction was SGLT2 inhibitors which are diabetes drugs. They work by blocking glucose reabsorption by the kidneys resulting in lower blood sugar and diuretic effects. The second class of drugs was estrogens which we saw in the drug specific analysis 24% reduction. The third PDA5 inhibitors like Viagra or Seialis 14% reduction. Statins had a very minor effect on mortality risk, only 3% reduction. Metformin had no effect, which is interesting because SGLT2 inhibitors had a massive effect. And ACE inhibitors, which are blood pressure medications, were associated with an 11% increased risk, probably because high blood pressure is quite lethal. The difference between metformin and SGLT2 inhibitors, is quite interesting. We've seen from previous human observational data that metformin doesn't reduce the risk of mortality in non-diabetics who are generally healthy. But metformin does reduce the risk of cancer, heart disease, and mortality in diabetics. There is a difference in metformin and sgt2 inhibitors. Metformin decreases hepatic glucose production and increases insulin sensitivity. SGLT2 inhibitors block glucose reabsorption in the kidneys which results in more excretion of glucose in the urine. When it comes to the cardio and kidney protective effects, then SGLT2 inhibitors haven't been seemed to be more effective than metformin. So, the reason why SGLT2 inhibitors appear to provide a greater reduction in mortality risk than metformin is because SGLT2 inhibitors also have systemic effects on the kidneys and heart, whereas metformin is mostly lowering blood sugar. There's also a big cost difference between metformin that costs only about $20 a month and SGLT2 inhibitors, which cost up to $400 or $500 a month. So there is a massive cost barrier. Next, let's talk about estrogen because estrogen pharmaceuticals were associated with decrease in mortality most commonly. This might be because estrogen levels drop close to zero after menopause. And this rapid decline in estrogen increases the risk of heart disease and frailty in women. Women who go on hormone replacement therapy and start taking estrogen appear to prolong the cardrotective and neuroprotective effects of estrogen. Men obviously aren't going to take estrogen because of the feminizing effects unless they really want to. However, there's an interesting study on mice that show that 17 alpha estradiol, which is a non-feminizing estrogen, extended male lifespan by 19% but not in female mice. So, this non-feminizing estrogen might extend male lifespan but not female lifespan because females already produce their own estrogen. It's too early to say if 17 alpha estradiol is going to extend lifespan in humans, but it's certainly very interesting. We do have clinical trials looking at the effects of hormone replacement therapy in women on the risk of all cause mortality, heart disease mortality, and cancer mortality. A 2017 meta analysis of randomized control trials saw that estrogen therapy had no effect on mortality, cancer, or heart disease mortality when used for a median of 5 to 7 years. However, younger post-menopausal women aged 50 to 59 might see a small reduction in mortality risk. So there's no strong evidence that hormone replacement therapy would increase your risk or decrease your risk of mortality in clinical trials, but based on the observational data from the study we use in this video, it is associated with reduced risk. The third class of drugs that provided significant benefits where erectile dysfunction medications like selenaphil, which is the main ingredient in Viagra. There are previous studies showing that PDE5 inhibitor use like Viagra or Seialis is associated with a lower risk of heart disease, Alzheimer's and all cause mortality among older men. That might be because PDE5 inhibitors have vasoddilating effects which means they lower blood pressure and improve blood flow which reduces the risk of heart disease and Alzheimer's. A 2023 meta analysis of 17 randomized control trials saw that selenaphil treatment improved cardiac function, pulmonary pressure, and exercise capacity in men aged 40 to 60. PD5 inhibitor use did show a trend towards reduced mortality in patients with pulmonary hypertension, but it wasn't statistically significant because of the small sample size. In type 2 diabetics, however, PDA5 inhibitor use is associated with a lower risk of all cause mortality. We definitely need more clinical trials on healthy individuals to see if PDF5 inhibitors have any mortality benefits or heart disease benefits in otherwise healthy people. I would presume that it's not going to work in younger populations. So something like younger than 60 years of age. But if you're older than 60, the natural process of aging has already started to decrease your blood flow and impair endothelial function, which is where these PD5 inhibitors can be quite useful to improve blood flow and lower blood pressure. There are a dozen more common supplements and compounds that have been seen to actually extend lifespan in the interventions testing program which is considered the gold standard for life extension experiments. Things like rapamycin have been seen to extend lifespan in mice in the ITP studies but there's no human data which is why it's not discussed in this video. Check out my video about the ITP test results next to see which supplements and compounds have potential to extend lifespan.

=== FILE: Creatine Megadose Challenge： Here's What My Labs Show [zWpjPz2cjgI].en.txt ===

About a month ago, I took 28 grams of creatine every day for a week to see how it affects my performance after sleep deprivation. I did notice some benefits. Besides the thumbnail, one of the most common questions I got asked was, "Isn't this bad for your kidneys?" RIP kidneys. Did you measure your kidney markers? Well, in this video, I'll share my kidney results before and after doing this experiment. I'll share the right and wrong kidney markers to focus on and what are the optimal ranges. Basically, I started taking creatine at the end of January before which I was taking zero creatine. I was taking the optimal standard dose of 100 milligrams per kilogram per day, which for me is 8 g and I did that for about 1 and 1/2 months. Then I took 28 g for a week in March and returned to 8 g a day until midappril. I was also taking 20 grams of creatine for about 3 to 5 days at the beginning of April when I was traveling. Here are my kidney results from January 2025, which is before I started taking creatine. As you can see, my kidneys are in perfect condition based on this test. Everything is in the optimal zone. eGFR 108, creatinine 0.95 mg per deciliter, uric acid 4.47 mg per deciliter, blood ura nitrogen 18.64 milligs per deciliter, cyin C 0.67 mg per liter, and sodium 141.5 millles per liter. Here are my kidney results in April, 3 months after taking creatine. eGFR 105, creatinine 0.97 milligs per deciliter, uric acid 5.17 mg per deciliter, blood ura nitrogen 19.69 milligs per deciliter, cyin C 0.65 mg per liter and sodium 140.9 millles per liter. Statistically speaking, everything is pretty much the same with no real difference. As you can see, my creatinine levels increased only slightly by 0.02 02 mg per deciliter, which is insignificant. And my eGFR dropped from 108 to 105, which is also insignificant. The reason for this might not have to do with creatine at all, because creatinine levels increase the more muscle you have. And between these three months, I went on a mini bulk and increased my weight from 79 kg to 83 kg. And I added at least 2 kg of muscle plus a little bit of fat. This was a deliberate bulk for me as I wanted to focus on strength training. and it's the ultimate reason I started taking creatine again. I'm going to share with you the optimal ranges for these kidney markers quite shortly. I knew that taking creatine wasn't going to mess up my kidneys, even if I did a large dose for a week. That's because creatine supplementation hasn't been seen to damage or reduce kidney function in otherwise healthy people. It's well established that creatine supplements are safe and they don't cause kidney damage. Only people with already existing kidney disease have to be careful with creatine. Even people doing resistance training and eating a high protein diet haven't seen creatine affect kidney function after 12 weeks. Kidney disease is usually caused by some other condition such as hypertension or high blood sugar. Creatin hasn't been seen to be a causal factor in causing kidney disease, but it can make things worse if you have poor kidney function. So, let's talk about how do you know if you have good kidney function. The most commonly used biomarker for kidney function is creatinin, which is not the same as creatine, although they sound similar. Creatinin is a byproduct of fossil creatine from protein metabolism or body protein breakdown. It means that if you eat more protein or you exercise, you'll have higher creatinin levels because you cause muscle damage during exercise. The issue is that if you're a person with slightly more muscle mass, you'll also have elevated creatinine levels because of that reason. You can see from studies that the more muscle mass and the higher your muscle strength, the higher your creatinine levels are. That's why creatinine isn't the best marker of kidney health in people who exercise or who have more muscle. This is why you saw my creatinine levels increase from 0.95 to 0.97 milligs per deciliter. It had nothing to do with creatine but more to do with the increase in my muscle mass. The normal reference range for serum creatinin is 0.74 to 1.35 mg per deciliter for men and 0.59 to 1.04 milligs per deciliter for women. So my result of 0.97 milligrams is in the optimal zone and in straight in the middle even though I was taking a lot of creatine and I have more muscle than the average person. But looking at only creatinine is very misleading. A better marker of kidney health is chattin C because it's not affected by muscle mass or exercise. Cistatin C is a protein found in all bodily tissues and fluids. With normal kidney function, glomeular filtration clears cyaten C levels from the blood. During kidney dysfunction, cyaten C levels rise. Normal cyaten C levels are 0.62 to 1.15 milligrams per liter. The higher the cyatin C levels, the worse your kidney health. My chattin C levels went from 0.67 to 0.65 milligs per liter, which is in the most optimal range. Based on all of this, my kidney function is very good, but not because of taking creatine. Creatine just doesn't have significant effects on kidney function if you're otherwise healthy. Your overall kidney function is assessed by eGFR, estimated glomeular filtration rate, which reflects how much blood passes through the tiny filters in the kidneys called the glomeuli that filter waste material from the blood. Normal eGFR levels are above 100. Anything below 100 indicates kidney problems and the lower the eGFR, the more advanced the stage of kidney disease. The problem is that eGFR is usually calculated from creatinin. And as we already know, creatinine levels can be often misleading. If you have more muscle mass, you exercise more, and you have more muscle strength. This might create a false interpretation of kidney dysfunction in otherwise healthy people. Instead, you should calculate eGFR from cyaten C because cistaten C is less sensitive to muscle mass. You can use the eGFR calculator at the National Kidney Foundation website, kidney.org, to calculate eGFR, and see the results for both creatinine and cyatin C. My eGFR based on my January results was 110 when calculated from creatinin and 129 when calculated from cistaten C and 123 when calculated from both. My eGFR based on my April results was 108 when calculated from creatinin and 130 when calculated from cistatin C and 123 when calculated from both. That's again an insignificant difference. So, as you can see, taking large amounts of creatine didn't have any real effects on my kidney function because my kidney markers were already pretty optimal to begin with. Someone with poor kidney function might have seen a different result. But overall, you don't have to take massive amounts of creatine. The optimal dose for maintenance purposes is 100 milligs per kilogram per day. And if you do experience some sleep deprivation every once in a while or you have jet lag, then you can take some larger doses of creatine, something like 0.35 g per kilogram, which for me was 28 g. === FILE: Did Scientists Just Make Old Monkeys Young Again [A2xUr4dk124].en.txt ===

Did scientists in China just make old monkeys young again? At least that's what a lot of social media headlines and articles claimed. In this video, I'm going to walk you through what the study actually found. And I'll also have Matt Cberlain share his thoughts, who's one of the world's leading bioertologists. The study was published in September 2025 in the journal Cell. They took aged Macaka vascularis, also known as crab eating macak, who were 19 to 23 years old. For humans, that would be the equivalent of 57 to 69 years. There were also younger monkeys who were used for comparison as the control group. The macak was chosen because they're quite similar to humans in physiology, genetics, and disease susceptibility. We share 93% of our DNA with them. The monkeys were injected with scinsesscent senoresistant human meenymal progenitor cells, SRC's derived from human embryionic stem cells. They gene edited the stem cells, specifically the FOXO3 gene, to introduce double mutations that resulted in higher FOX3 expression. Foxo3 is a gene that seemed to have longevity effects in animals and in humans. The longest living humans have higher FOX3A expression. FOX3A is a gene that regulates stress resistance and resilience. Basically making the organism more resilient against stress, exercise, and energy deprivation. So we know that stem cell function is important for biological aging. Stem cell dysregulation is one of the hallmarks of aging. And we know that loss of stem cell function in different tissues and organs during aging can contribute to declines in the function of those organs as well as declines in our ability to heal from wounds. It's a little bit less clear how big the effects will be for lifespan and health span by restoring or even boosting stem cell function. There really haven't been any compelling studies in mice showing that you can robustly increase lifespan through stem cell therapies. Probably also worth saying there's no evidence in humans that stem cell therapies promote longevity despite the fact that there are lots of clinics out there um giving these sorts of therapies. Um, there have been a couple of studies in rodents using exoomes from young animals that have reported increases in lifespan or improvements in health span. It seems plausible that those exoomes are stem cell derived, although that hasn't really been definitively shown. So, I think what we can say at this point with confidence is stem cells are part of the aging process or I should say I think what we can say with confidence is that stem cell dysregulation is part of the aging process. But we really don't know at this point how large the effect would be if we could prevent stem cell dysregulation or even boost it beyond normal levels in aged animals or aged people. The other old monkeys got either saline water or they were injected with human stem cells that weren't genetically edited with FOX3. The monkeys received their treatment every 2 weeks into the arm vein for a total of 44 weeks or 11 months which for humans would be the equivalent of 3 years. The dose was 2 million cells per kilogram of body weight, which is similar to the doses in human clinical trials. The scientists did comprehensive before and after testing on the old monkeys. They did routine blood tests, cognitive tests, morphometric analysis, and medical imaging. In total, they analyzed 61 tissues across 10 systems and also measured epigenetic age scores. What they found after 44 weeks was that their biological clock scores decreased by about 2 to 7 years which in humans would be the equivalent of 6 to 15 years. Their brain function improved. They saw about 30 to 40% improvement in accuracy and latency. Their cortical thickness in the brain was 3 to 5 years younger after the treatment. Their myelin density that protects neurons was 25 to 30% higher. And they saw a reduction in amalloid and toao which are implicated in neurodeeneration. Their bone mass increased by about 10 to 20%. Their reproductive health improved by about 20 to 40%. They saw about 35% reduction in skin scinessence and 30 to 50% reduction in peripheral blood monuclear cell scinessence. Out of the all organs analyzed, 54% of them improved and overall the treatment was safe and well tolerated. While these results sound quite impressive, they have to be taken with a grain of salt. I think people should appreciate that this paper did not actually show a reduction in biological age despite what they claimed. This is a little bit of a larger problem in the field is that many people are just making up their own definition of biological aging and then claiming a reduction. In this case, unfortunately, the editors allowed that into the paper. Um, what they did do was create their own epigenetic and transcriptional clocks that correlate with age. And what they showed was that the FOX3 engineered stem cells could have an impact on those custommade clocks in the direction that would be consistent with lower biological age. There are a couple of reasons to be a little bit skeptical of the clocks used here. Um, they were built off of very very small sample sizes. So, I think they only had about eight animals per group. Typically, when you're building biological age estimators, you would use orders of magnitude more individuals to create your clocks. So, in some ways, this is a very preliminary result. It's consistent with the idea that the engineered stem cells were causing the epiggenome and the transcriptto shift back towards something that looks more like a youthful state. But it certainly is not definitive for a reduction in biological age or a reversal of biological aging. >> Unfortunately, the authors of the study didn't provide any external images or before and after photos of the monkeys. So, we don't know if they actually looked younger. I'm pretty sure that they actually didn't look younger. One of the biggest fears people have about taking creatine is that it causes hair loss. However, there's never been a study that actually looked at it until now. A new 2025 study looked at creatine's effects on hair loss and DHT levels. And they found that 5 g of creatine for 12 weeks had no effect on hair growth, thickness, or density compared to placebo. There was also no difference in testosterone or DHT levels, which is thought to cause hair loss. So, at this dose, creatine doesn't cause hair loss. However, there are some people that swear that after taking creatine, they lost some hair. This might be because of genetic predispositions or their baseline DHT levels. 20 years ago, there was a study that saw that creatine did raise DHT levels in rugby players whose DHT levels were low to begin with. They also used 25 g of creatine for 7 days, followed by 5 g for 14 days. This study didn't look at hair loss, but they saw DHT levels rising 56% in those who had low baseline DHT. So, creatine doesn't raise your DHT if your DHD is normal, but it might if it's low. DHD is thought to be one of the reasons why some men lose their hair. They're genetically sensitive to the hair loss effects of DHD. Overall, there's no evidence that creatine would cause hair loss, but not everyone reacts the same way to creatine. Follow for more.

It means they lost 80% of those 3 kg as muscle and only 20% as fat. sleeping 8.5 hours resulted in 1.4 kg of fat loss and 1.5 kg of muscle loss. They lost pretty much 50/50 muscle and fat, which is quite normal for regular weight loss without exercise. It means that if you're putting a lot of effort into your workouts, but you're not sleeping enough, you might end up losing more muscle than fat. === FILE: How Bad Is Vaping？ [KcjCccdUO8I].en.txt ===

the tobacco industry is saying that vaping is safe what they don't say is that you're still increasing your risk of asthma lung injury and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease it is considered to be somewhat safer than regular smoking because the Vape contains less toxins than regular smoke the Royal College of general practitioners from England has stated that ecigarettes are unlikely to exceed 5% of the harm from conventional smoking that's quite a bold statement and if it were to be true then it means that vaping is 95% safer than regular smoking however the FDA hasn't approved any ecigarette as a smoking sensation device and it hasn't authorized to make any claims about risk reduction compared to regular cigarettes vaping is associated with an increased risk of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease bronchitis and Asthma even among those who have never smoked regular cigarettes yes vaping is safer than regular smoking but it doesn't come without any health risks whether or not vaping is going to increase your mortality or give you cancer we don't know because it's such a new thing and we don't have any long-term study

=== FILE: How Does Alcohol Affect Your Sleep [SgnnUY9unjI].en.txt ===

alcohol is often used for Stress Management and falling asleep however alcohol at any doses has a substantial effect on your Sleep Quality as shown by a recent metaanalysis they analyzed 27 studies and found that low doses less than 050 G per kilogram alcohol reduced REM sleep which is when dreaming occurs if you weigh 80 kg like me then that will be the equivalent of 40 G of alcohol for comparison a glass of wine or a can of beer has about 14 G of alcohol even a doses of 0.35 5 G per kogam alcohol increased REM sleep onset latency which means you fell into dreaming much later at larger doses of over 0.85 G per kogam alcohol reduced sleep onset latency which means that it took less time to fall asleep for me that would be the equivalent of 68 G of alcohol which I would get from around five drinks overall it seems that alcohol has a much more negative effect on your Sleep Quality if you drink more than five drinks it makes you fall asleep faster but the quality of asleep is worse because you get less REM sleep REM sleep is when dreams and memory consolidation occurs so you don't want to miss that if you do drink then stick to much smaller amounts of alcohol such as less than 0.35 G per kilogram which you would get from around two drinks follow for more

how to properly wash vegetables I know this a serious issue people don't know how to wash their vegetables properly here's why it's important if you don't wash your vegetables you're going to miss all the pesticides dirt insects hiding in your food first soak your vegetables in salt water with vinegar the salt will dehydrate and kill all the bacteria on the food the vinegar can help to remove pesticides and other chemicals then leave them in a bowl with a mix for about 2 to 3 minutes after that rinse them in a bowl with clean water you should also wash your apples if you buy them from the store they're usually covered in wax soak the apples in a mix of baking soda and vinegar for about 10 minutes this is going to remove the wax and you can actually see it later in the water fruit and vegetables are incredibly important for your health but you still want to protect yourself from ingesting the wrong thing by learning how to wash them properly

Moving on with the peptides that target the brain. Epitalin is a synthetic tetrapeptide. It's considered a bioregulator, a molecule that mimics the body's own short peptides to regulate gene expression, tissue repair, and regeneration. Epitalin was discovered by a Russian researcher, Dr. Vladimir Havinson. He's also the person leading the most research on epitalin. In 2002, a clinical trial in Russia on 162 patients with retinitis pigmentosa, a genetic condition of progressive retinal degeneration and vision loss, saw that epitalin could improve visual acuity, and 64.8% of them broadened the total visual field by 90 to 120 degrees. They injected 5 micrograms per eye, parabulberly, for 10 consecutive days. None of the epitalin-treated patients experienced side effects. A 2020 study saw that sublingual epitalin at a dose of 0.5 mg a day for 20 days, in 75 women, improved melatonin production, through modulation of the circadian clock system. It's been also shown to do that in elderly people and old monkeys. Epitalin activates chromatin, which is a mass of DNA in your brain that regulates the circadian rhythm. To be honest, this is the most exciting and interesting thing about epitalin. If epitalin is able to counteract the circadian clock dysfunction that happens with aging, it could potentially also help with a lot of neurodegenerative conditions. I've shared on the channel before that the circadian clock dysfunction will eventually be considered a new hallmark of aging, but epitalin does a lot more than that. In human cells, epitalin extends telomere length. However, it can do so in both cancer cells and normal cells. In this study, epitalin at a dose of 0.1 to 1 microgram per milliliter extended cancer telomeres by 4 to 8 kilobases within 4 days. Normal cell telomeres extended by about 1.45 fold after 3 weeks. In tuberculosis patients, epitalin has been seen to reduce chromosomal aberrations and stabilize the genome, but not fully reverse genome fragility. Epitalin basically didn't correct the structural aberrations associated with telomere shortening from tuberculosis, but it had some protective effects against future damage. Epitalin increases neurogenesis the growth of brain cells in human gingival mesenchymal stem cells. This explains the reason why epitalin affects things like telomere length and melatonin synthesis, as well as circadian rhythm regulation. Even getting epitalin intranasally increases neuronal activity in rats by up to 2 to 2.5 times, as epitalin easily crosses the blood-brain barrier. These sound all very interesting and speculative, but would epitalin make you live longer? In mice, epitalin treatment does extend maximum lifespan by 12.3%, but not the mean lifespan. The last 10% of the survivors live 13.3% longer. There's also no difference in overall cancer rate, although leukemia was six-fold lower compared to the control mice in this study. There is a prospective study on elderly Russian and Ukrainian adults over the age of 60. They were given epitalin and thymoline for 2 to 3 years, and they were followed up for 6 to 8 years. Those who received these peptides saw improved physiological function and experienced a 2 to 2.4x lower incidence of heart disease, hypertension, osteoporosis, and osteoarthritis. Their mortality was also lower. The group who got thymoline alone had about 2 times lower mortality compared to controls. Epithelamine alone had 1.6 to 1.8 times lower risk. The combination of thymoline and epithelamine, 2.5x lower, and annual treatment for 6 years, 4.1x lower. Another prospective study with a 15-year follow-up on 39 coronary heart disease patients who received epitalin saw that they had 50% lower rate of heart disease mortality, 50% lower cardiovascular failure, and 28% lower rate of overall mortality. They did have better circadian rhythm regulation, lower cholesterol, and better physical function than people not receiving the treatment. Now, these results sound quite astonishing, and they are astonishing if they were to be true. We don't know necessarily how true these results are, because these studies have several limitations. Number one, they're not randomized controlled trials, so they're mostly observational, and we don't know the full methodology or the data set. We don't know how these individuals were randomized or if randomized at all, and how were they treated. Second of all, the research is done in Russia, led by Dr. Havinson. He's also the one who owns patents to the epitalin, so there is conflict of interest here. The guy who discovered this peptide also owns the patents to this peptide, and his studies get these amazing results. It just means that we would need to reproduce these studies in other populations, in other countries, by other researchers, to see if those effects are actually true. Overall, my rating for epitalin is 4 out of 5. I think it has a lot of promise if you look at the mechanistic evidence and the preclinical evidence. And you can't deny that at least it has quite a lot of human studies, even though those studies can be somewhat limited. Next, we have a mitochondrial peptide called MOTS-C. MOTS-C, or mitochondrial ORF, of the 12-S RNA type C, is a mitochondrial-derived peptide composed of 16 amino acids encoded by the 12-S RNA region of the mitochondrial genome. It gets activated during metabolic stress in the nucleus, and it activates AMPK, which is an energy sensor that's been seen to be good for longevity. Because of its role in the mitochondria, it balances inflammation, improves glucose metabolism, muscle function, and overall redox balance. As a result, it might improve insulin resistance, heart disease, and overall aging. Obese mice fed a high-fat diet, see reduced insulin resistance when given MOTS-C. In type 2 diabetic mice, MOTS-C restores mitochondrial function in the heart and improves glucose levels. In obese humans, circulating MOTS-C levels are decreased, and low MOTS-C levels are associated with insulin resistance in humans. MOTS-C levels are also lower in kidney disease patients and people with liver disease. Interestingly, MOTS-C levels are similar between obese and normal weight individuals. So it seems that only age and insulin resistance lowers MOTS-C levels, but obesity doesn't do that. This study showed that MOTS-C levels decline with age in mice, and they're lower in humans with diabetes. In aged and diabetic mouse models, systemic treatment with MOTS-C reduced beta-cell senescence markers in pancreatic islets and improved glucose control. The authors propose that MOTS-C acts by suppressing mTORC1 signaling, which is the body's growth switch, and by doing that, it preserves mitochondrial function and beta-cell health. This doesn't necessarily mean that MOTS-C would fix diabetes, but it might mean that people with diabetes or they're obese probably aren't exercising enough, so which is the reason why they have lower MOTS-C levels. People who are exercising and they're otherwise lean have higher MOTS-C because they're engaged in physical activity. In fact, there is human evidence that serum MOTS-C positively correlates with lower body strength, lower body power, and muscle mass, although not aerobic capacity. In mice and humans, exercise increases MOTS-C levels. In this study, 10 healthy young men did high-intensity interval cycling, 10 rounds of 60 seconds at peak power, and their MOTS-C levels in their skeletal muscle increased 11.9-fold immediately after the exercise and it remained elevated for 4 hours afterwards. Circulating plasma MOTS-C increased 1.6-fold during exercise and 1.5-fold immediately after exercise. So the argument for using MOTS-C as a peptide is that it's like an exercise in a bottle. You increase MOTS-C levels as if you were exercising, and then MOTS-C has benefits on your metabolism and overall health. My first reaction to this is that why wouldn't you just exercise then, because it's a lot cheaper and safer. Now, of course, it would be cool to have a literal exercise in a bottle. Maybe you can exercise a bit less, you can cut your exercise in half and get the same benefits. Maybe MOTS-C has these kinds of effects. But of course, it could also apply to certain situations where you can't exercise, such as the elderly population or if you're hospitalized. And lastly, injecting MOTS-C as a peptide probably raises MOTS-C levels a lot more than exercise does, at least in the short term. Exercise will still raise MOTS-C levels more in the skeletal muscle, but in the plasma, injecting MOTS-C would probably result in higher MOTS-C levels. Interestingly, MOTS-C is a myostatin inhibitor. Myostatin is a protein that stops your body from building muscle. Exercise inhibits myostatin, and part of that might be because of increased MOTS-C levels. So MOTS-C could help to prevent muscle loss during aging. There's also mechanistic evidence that MOTS-C can help with bone growth and osteoporosis. Exercise does so as well, obviously, and MOTS-C might mediate some of those effects. MOTS-C doesn't have any human clinical trials. Here's what we do know. MOTS-C levels are decreased in people with diabetes and other metabolic diseases. MOTS-C in mice improves insulin sensitivity and glucose tolerance. MOTS-C levels increase during exercise. People who exercise have higher MOTS-C. MOTS-C might mediate some of the benefits of exercise on muscle growth, insulin sensitivity, and bone growth. My overall rating for MOTS-C based on animal research is 4 out of 5, but because there are no human studies, I'll have to give you the 3 out of 5. Humanin is a 24-aminoacid mitochondrial-derived peptide that improves mitochondrial function, inflammation, and metabolism. The most common effect of humanin is that it protects the brain against inflammation and oxidative stress. That's because the brain has a lot of mitochondria. In mice, humanin prevents age-related cognitive decline, and in humans, humanin levels are associated with better cognitive function. In humans, humanin levels are lower in Alzheimer's patients than in healthy controls, and low mitochondrial DNA copy number is also associated with lower humanin levels. It means that people who are unhealthier have lower humanin. There are no human studies looking at the effects of humanin for Alzheimer's or dementia. So there is some preclinical data showing that humanin might help with neurodegeneration, but there's no human studies yet. And humanin treatment in mice is seen to be associated with lower IGF-1 levels. Lower IGF-1 levels are associated with greater longevity in humans, as well as animals. Younger than 66 years of age have higher humanin than older individuals. Overall, my rating for humanin is 3 out of 5. It's a similar situation as with MOTC. Unfortunately, it doesn't have any human clinical trials. One of the most promising and interesting brain peptides is cerebrolysine. It's a mix of different peptides and brain growth factors that could help with neurodegenerative conditions. In fact, cerebrolysine has been in clinical use for 30 years. It's used in some countries, but is not necessarily government-approved. Cerebrolysine has neuroprotective effects by improving inflammation, blood flow to the brain, and thrombolytic effects that reduces blood-brain barrier permeability. A 2019 Cochrane review of six studies saw that cerebrolysine treatment had beneficial effects on memory and thinking and daily functioning. There was no reported risk of side effects with the treatment. There's no evidence that cerebrolysine would prevent Alzheimer's, treat it, or improve cognition in otherwise healthy individuals. A 2023 Cochrane review of seven Randomness Control Trial found that cerebrolysine after a stroke doesn't reduce mortality rates either. So cerebrolysine seems to improve cognition recovery in the short term, but its effects over the long term are limited. A 2023 systematic review of 10 studies on cerebrolysine for traumatic brain injury showed short-term neurological improvements, but no benefit on mortality or hospitalization either. Overall, my rating for cerebrolysine is 4.5 out of 5. It's hard to say if most supplements work because you might not feel anything. But there are several supplements that I've noticed to change some of my biomarkers, my fitness, or just how I feel. So, in this video, I'm going to share these supplements. The first supplement is HMBB, which is a byproduct of the amino acid leucine. There's research that supplementing 1.5 to three grams a day of HMBB can increase muscle mass and strength, especially in older individuals, by reducing protein breakdown. A 2022 umbrella review of 15 systematic reviews concluded that HMBB supplementation doesn't increase muscle mass or strength in healthy individuals, but it has benefits in individuals who aren't getting enough protein. The reason I saw benefits from taking HMBB is because I was taking it while I was in a fasted state in the morning. And fasting by definition is the absence of protein. Even when I was eating around 160 g of protein in my eating window later in the day, I have a smaller eating frequency and I have two protein meals per day. Taking HMBB in the morning in the fastest state in my experience helped with muscle growth by reducing muscle breakdown. Not by a massive amount, but whenever I was taking HMBB in the past, I noticed bigger muscle definition and size. I probably wouldn't see this effect if I was eating breakfast and several protein meals throughout the day. However, HMBB might still be beneficial for elderly people. A 2025 meta analysis of 21 randomized control trials on adults over the age of 50 did see significant improvements in muscle mass, strength, and gate speed from taking 3 g a day of HMBB for at least 12 weeks. So, if you're over the age of 50, you might benefit from HMBB supplementation. Or if you're doing some form of intermittent fasting, you could also benefit from that. === FILE: I Took Melatonin Pre-Workout — The Science Blew My Mind [wY_wGTWhuQs].en.txt ===

Most people think of melatonin as just a sleep hormone and more recently as a powerful antioxidant. But what if I told you that taking melatonin pre-workout could increase your growth hormone by 157%. That's exactly what a study from 2007 saw. Now, I'm not talking about turning into a gigach because that's not what growth hormone does. But this surge in growth hormone has benefits on recovery and body composition which I'm going to talk about in this video. The study was published in 2007. They took 60 healthy young physically active men and women and randomly divided them into taking either 0.5 milligrams or 5 milligrams of melatonin and compared it to a 1 milligram placebo pill. They measured their growth hormone at baseline. By minute 40 after ingestion, growth hormone rose by 157% from baseline in the 5 milligram group and by 106% in the 0.5 mig group. While the placebo saw no significant effect. Then at the 60-minute mark, the participants all did 20 minutes of leg press resistance training. By that time, growth hormone levels from the melatonin had already began to decrease slightly. About 25 minutes after the exercise had started, growth hormone levels in the 5 mg group had raised again to 132% and in the 0.5 mg group to 106% above baseline. Basically, exercise bumped back up the growth hormone because exercise also raises growth hormone. However, in the placebo group, exercise raised growth hormone by only 30% above baseline, which confirms melatonin's effect on raising growth hormone. Typically, you would expect exercise to raise growth hormone by about 50 to 70%, which is less than half than the 5 mg group alone. Afterwards, growth hormone levels began trickling down to baseline. This is a very interesting study. It shows that melatonin can raise growth hormone independent of the time of day. The reason for this is because melatonin inhibits somatin, which is a growth hormone inhibiting hormone. It's no coincidence that the largest surges in growth hormone happen in the first hours of sleep, especially deep sleep. And it looks like that this surge in growth hormone is more dependent on melatonin rather than sleep itself. As this study showed that taking melatonin at any time of the day will raise growth hormone. Now, a surge in growth hormone by 150 or even 300% doesn't mean as much as you think it does. Growth hormone's effects on muscle growth are overrated. In fact, growth hormone alone has no effect on muscle growth. Growth hormones effects on muscle mass are mediated through increasing IGF-1 levels or insulin like growth factor 1. Growth hormone from the pituitary gland in the brain signals the liver to produce IGF-1 that then has anabolic effects on bones, muscles, and other tissues. So, did melatonin have any effect on IGF-1? Neither of the melatonin doses 0.5 and 5 milligrams nor resistance exercise had a significant effect on serum IGF-1 levels during the two-hour study window. That's because the rise of IGF-1 from growth hormone takes several hours up to 12 to 24 hours. So it is biologically plausible that the melatonin intervention did result in higher IG of 1 in 12 to 24 hours, although it wasn't measured in this study. Exercise is known to raise IGF-1, but it takes longer than two hours for the growth hormone to signal IGF-1 production, which is why exercise wasn't seen to raise IG of 1 in this study either. So, what does it mean? Does it mean that you should start popping melatonin before your workouts? Unfortunately, we don't have a lot of other studies looking at the effects of pre-workout melatonin on exercise performance. In a few studies, taking melatonin 30 minutes before high-intensity training, reduces markers of oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation, which is the oxidation of fats and enhances immune function. Melatonin at a dose of 6 mg taken 30 minutes before aerobic exercise, also increases carbohydrate metabolism, which means their glucose uptake into the cells was higher. In rats, melatonin 30 minutes before exhaustive exercise has been seen to improve endurance and accelerate muscle glycogen replenishment within the next 48 hours. Now, those effects aren't massive, but they are statistically significant. And we don't know what kind of an effect would the 157% increase in growth hormone have on body composition or muscle growth. I think the effects would be greater than zero, but probably not massive. I guess someone just has to try it out. And by that someone, I mean me. And by me, I mean yes, I did try it out for a few workouts. So, I took 5 milligrams of melatonin 1 hour before resistance training. And I did feel slightly nauseous and a little bit tired, especially after the workout. Feeling slightly more tired didn't reduce my performance. I was still as strong as was before, but I did feel a bit more tired during the workout. And I felt especially tired after the workout. Now, you can try it out for yourself. Maybe you don't get that effect because melatonin is incredibly safe. But I don't see myself using pre-workout melatonin on a regular basis. maybe occasionally, but this 157% increase in growth hormone isn't that much. It's worth noting that you shouldn't get caught up with the growth hormone, as a lot of people do. Fasting is notoriously known to raise growth hormone. If you fast for 24 hours, growth hormone has been seen to rise by 210% on average and do so 70% more frequently compared to eating regularly. But if you're not eating, then you're not going to be able to build muscle and be anabolic. You need to eat to build muscle. Fasting can just signal your body to preserve the lean tissue. That's what growth hormone does. Growth hormone increases during fasting so that your body would reduce muscle protein breakdown and increase fat oxidation and fat breakdown. So the growth hormone is a signal for your body to lose fat and maintain muscle. That's why exercise increases growth hormone. That's why sleep increases growth hormone. === FILE: If You're Older Than 25, You Need to Watch This [fhmhn48hizU].en.txt ===

Most people think aging starts somewhere in their 40s when the gray hair shows up, the back starts aching, or the weight doesn't come off like it used to. But the truth is, aging starts a lot sooner, already in your early 20s. You just don't notice it. In this video, I'll reveal the hidden aspects of aging that already start in your early 20s. And more importantly, what you can do to slow it down. The first thing that starts declining is your cardiorespiratory fitness, which reflects in your V2 max. It peaks when you're 20 years old and steadily decreases after that. A higher V2 max above 50 milliliters per kilogram per minute is associated with a lower risk of mortality and a V2 max below 17 means you've lost physical independence and you can't do everyday activities without assistance. V2 max is a matter of use it or lose it. If you don't do cardiovascular exercise and you don't train your V2 max, it's going to decrease. And the faster it decreases, the higher your risk of future heart disease, dementia, and all cause mortality. To increase your V2 max, you need to do aerobic training or high-intensity interval training. High-intensity interval training is more time effective, but it's recommended to do both because they train different systems. However, you shouldn't do just low inensity cardio or endurance training. That's because with age you see a decline in fast twitch muscle fibers that can be trained only with lifting weights at near maximum intensities, jumping, sprinting, or high-intensity training. The reason these fast twitch muscle fibers are important is that they help you to maintain agility and speed. When you get older, if you fall off the stairs, you can break a hip and die. And if you're slow, you're not able to catch yourself or you're not able to maintain balance fast enough. You're more likely to just fall. It means that by sprinting or lifting something at near maximum intensities like Olympic weightlifting, you maintain fast twitch muscle fibers that help you to maintain more muscle and a better metabolism as you age. It's been seen that the elderly people who do just endurance training have much fewer fast twitch muscle fibers, whereas those who do strength training have significantly more. When it comes to overall muscle mass and muscle strength, then you can get away with not lifting weights until your 40s. That's because natural muscle mass and strength peak between the ages of 30 and 40 in men and in early 40s in women. Having low muscle mass later in life is a predictor of death from all causes. That's because with low muscle, you're at a higher risk of diabetes, obesity, Alzheimer's, and falling off the stairs. However, when you compare muscle mass and muscle strength, then muscle strength is a stronger predictor of mortality than muscle mass. And usually if you have good muscle strength, you already have adequate amounts of muscle mass. And when you compare muscle strength and muscle power, then muscle power is even stronger of a predictor of mortality than strength. === FILE: Is Fatty15 Worth It？ Breaking Down C15 Supplements [tvvDc0gufYA].en.txt ===

I've been getting dozens of requests to make a video about fatty 15. Fatty 15 is a new supplement that contains C15 or pentadonoic acid, which is a fatty acid found in dairy fat like cheese and milk. C15 is marketed as a critical nutrient needed for good health and longevity because it will strengthen cell membranes and increase mitochondrial function. The price point, $50 a month. That's not cheap and actually quite expensive. So, the effects of the supplement better be worth it for this price point. I'm going to look at the research behind C15 and see if it's actually what it's claimed to be. Like I said, you naturally get C-15 from dairy fats and whole fat dairy like whole milk, cheese, cottage cheese, yogurt, cafir, etc. There are observational studies showing that elevated plasma C-15 levels are associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and some cancers. This 2021 meta analysis of 18 observational studies saw that higher C-15 levels were associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular disease. Now, these are all very fascinating findings that people with higher C-15 levels have less heart disease and diabetes. Because humans can't make much C15 endogenously, the main reason for elevated C-15 levels could be because of consuming dairy fat. However, there are also other possibilities. For example, otherwise healthy people tend to have lower inflammation status. And we know that high inflammation tends to oxidize certain fatty acids in the bloodstream. It might be kind of a survivorship bias that the individuals with the highest C-15 levels have the lowest inflammation and the best metabolic health, which is the real reason why they see a lower risk of heart disease. Yes, they would still have to eat dairy, but the individuals who eat a lot of dairy and have low C-15 levels might also have high inflammation that lowers their C-15 levels. Unfortunately, we don't have that kind of research to look at it. That's why we would also have to look at the clinical trials that look at the effects of C-15 on metabolic health in isolation and in a controlled environment. Fortunately, there are at least two clinical trials on C-15. The first one is done by the companies selling fatty 15 and it was published in 2024. They took overeight individuals and saw that taking 200 milligs a day of C15 for 12 weeks rose plasma C-15 levels significantly compared to placebo. So yes, taking C-15 as a supplement raises plasma C-15 levels. Those whose plasma C-15 reached over 5 micrograms per milliliter saw a statistically significant decrease in liver enzymes, ALT minus 29 units per liter, A minus 6, and GGGTUS 111 units per liter. Their hemoglobin also increased by 0.6 g per deciliter. However, only 50% of the people out of 20 reached plasma C15 over 5 micrograms per milliliter. and those who didn't reach that threshold didn't see any improvements. That's 50% of the people getting the supplement not getting any benefits. The reason why half of the participants didn't reach the required threshold was thought to be that they weren't taking the supplement consistently. But it might be some other reason for it as well. So based on this study, C-15 levels only rise in certain people after taking the supplement, not everyone. And two, to get the benefits from C15 supplementation, you need to reach plasma C-15 levels of over five micrograms per deciliter. And if you don't reach that threshold, you're not seeing any benefits. Furthermore, the participants saw no difference in their cholesterol, glucose, and inflammation. That's probably because their levels were within normal range to begin with, whereas that wasn't the case with their liver enzymes. These overate people already had elevated liver enzymes in the beginning. So C15 supplementation might work only in improving markers that are not optimal and it might work only in some people and not others. Another 2024 randomized control trial saw that C15 supplementation together with a Mediterranean style diet resulted in a significantly greater decrease in LDL cholesterol compared to just the diet protocol without C-15. However, the addition of C-15 to the diet didn't produce additional benefits on lowering total cholesterol, triglycerides, liver enzymes, insulin, and homir. The participants had these markers higher than normal, which could explain the effects, but the improvements in them were already achievable with a Mediterranean style diet with C-15 providing no additional benefits. The diet prescribed in this trial did include some dairy, but they recommended low-fat dairy and they recommended restricting other animal fats. So, they weren't getting a lot of C15 from their dietary sources. And based on this finding, it's not clear whether C15 supplementation would provide any additional benefits that you wouldn't get from an otherwise healthy diet, even if that healthy diet is low in dairy fats and other animal fats. And that's pretty much it. There's only two clinical trials that I could find on C-15 supplementation. So, let me give you a recap of the findings. Number one, C-15 supplementation raises plasma C-15 levels and higher C-15 levels are associated with a lower risk of heart disease and diabetes. However, because these are observational studies, we don't know if supplemental C-15 has the same effects. Number two, C15 supplementation doesn't raise plasma C-15 levels in everyone. And to get benefits, you need to reach a plasma C-15 level of over 5 micrograms per milliliter. Number three, C15 supplementation has no significant effect on cholesterol, blood sugar, insulin, or other markers of metabolic health compared to placebo or a standard Mediterranean diet. It might have additional effects on LDL cholesterol compared to diet alone. And number four, C15 supplementation lowers liver enzymes only if they're high to begin with and only in those people who reach a plasma C-15 of over 5 micrograms per milliliter. So overall, the evidence for C-15 supplementation is very limited and weak. Most of the claims that C15 is an essential nutrient and is very important for health and longevity is done by the company that sells fatty 15. So you have to take it with a massive grain of salt. The clinical evidence for C15 is very limited and it doesn't appear to provide any additional benefits that you wouldn't get from an otherwise healthy diet such as a healthy Mediterranean diet, even if that diet is low in dairy fats. Yes, the observational data is interesting that people who have higher plasma C-15 levels, they have less heart disease. That's very interesting indeed, but it's not clear whether this is because of consuming more C-15 from diet or supplements, or it might be because of something else, such as lower inflammation. We just don't have enough clinical data to make any conclusive claims about C-15. And for a monthly price tag of $50, I just think that it's not worth it to spend that much money on a speculative supplement. However, there are at least 15 supplements that do have a lot of evidence for longevity. Check out my video about this

A lot of people suffer from excess visceral fat because it accumulates around the organs and you can't see it with your bare eyes. I've managed to reduce my visceral fat from 359 g, which is already below average, to below 100 g, which is extremely low and optimal. One of the small tweaks I made to help me achieve such low viseral fat was adding green tea to my diet. Green tea, in my opinion, is one of the healthiest beverages in the world if you consume it in the right amounts and at the right time. So, in this video, I'm going to share how adding one to two cups of green tea per day can eviscerate visceral fat. The reason I started drinking green tea was because there's plenty of research suggesting that it helps to target specifically visceral fat. There's a 2012 randomiz control trial showing that kathagen enriched green tea for 12 weeks resulted in greater visceral fat loss than in the placebo group. The kathagen group lost 9.5 square cm of visceral fat on average compared to the 0.6 six square cm of the control group, which wasn't significant. The participants who drank kaggen enriched green tea lost 6.23% of their visceral fat compared to only 0.38% in the control group. That's 5.85% greater reduction in visceral fat for the green tea group. The kagen group consumed 350 ml of green tea with 609.3 mg of kagens and 68.6 mg of caffeine. Whereas the control group consumed only 86.2 mg of kagens and 40.4 millig of caffeine. So green tea high in kagens is more effective than green tea low in calagins. Another 2009 study found that green tea collagens enhanced the loss of abdominal fat from exercise. The green tea group lost 6.2% of abdominal subcutaneous fat whereas the control group gained 0.8%. Total abdominal area decreased 7.7% compared to 0.3% and intraabdominal fat reduced 8.7% compared to 1.4%. They consumed 500 ml of green tea with 625 mg of kadagens compared to zero in the control group and both groups consumed 39 mg of caffeine. A 2024 meta analysis of 24 studies saw that exercise plus green tea results in a small but statistically significant bonus reduction in fat mass of about 1 to 1.5 kg compared to exercise alone. So whenever you are exercising and trying to lose fat then drinking green tea on top of that makes you lose a little bit more extra fat especially visceral fat and intraabdominal fat. The reason green tea helps with visceral fat loss is because of its kagen content. In green tea, the specific is EGCG. === FILE: Longevity Drug Billionaires Take to Live Longer [6t1B9UbC5Gs].en.txt ===

billionaires are investing hundreds of millions of dollars into longevity research however there's currently One supplement that almost all the billionaires are taking to slow down their aging it's metformin which is a drug used to treat diabetes in diabetics metformin does reduce the risk of cardiovascular and all cause mortality significantly but what about otherwise healthy people in 2014 there was an observational study that suggested that diabetics taking metformin could live 15% longer than non-diabetics not taking metformin this is why a lot of biohackers and Longevity enthusiasts are taking metformin off label however the problem with this study was that it's an observational study and they didn't control for the other variables a recent 2022 reassessment of the 2014 study found that metformin was found to be associated with increased mortality across all levels of cumulative use meaning that no matter the dose metformin use was linked to a higher mortality risk primarily because metformine users had diabetes and diabetics generally have shorter life expectancy so as of now there is no evidence that metformin would extend the lifespan in human follow more
