=== FILE: Longevity for Normal People： Healthier Than the 95% [nKgr84cLQLw].en.txt ===

You don't have to spend thousands of dollars on blood tests, supplements, and different gadgets. There are a lot of things you can measure at home for free or for minimal cost. In this video, I'm going to give you the most fundamental longevity tests you can do that have a very high predictive value for your overall long-term health. Number one, waist circumference. A high waist circumference is indicative of excess visceral fat around the organs. It looks like this round belly. In fact, you could be otherwise with skinny arms and legs. But if you have a round belly, it's a sign of poor metabolic health and excess visceral fat. A 2014 study on over 650,000 people saw that waist circumference was linearly associated with an increased risk in all cause mortality in both men and women. The lowest risk was observed at 85 cm or 33.5 in in men and 65 cm or 25.5 in in women. A waist circumference of 100 cm or 39 in in men and 75 cm or 29.5 in in women is still acceptable but not optimal. So you want to get your waist circumference as low as possible. Number two, grip strength. Grip strength can be considered a good marker of upper body strength and overall health. Low grip strength correlates with type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, sarcopenia, frailty, liver disease, dementia, some cancers and all cause mortality. Your midlife grip strength already predicts how well are you going to do with everyday tasks 25 years later. Those with the lowest grip strength are three times more likely to have difficulties eating and rising from a chair. They're also twice as likely to have problems with putting on clothes independently. You don't have to train your grip strength directly to live longer. But a weak grip strength indicates overall low muscle mass and muscle strength. A strong grip is an indicator of good muscle strength that predicts lower mortality in the future. You can measure your grip strength with a dynamometer, which is a device that you squeeze as hard as possible to get a score. The stronger your grip, the higher your score. Grip strength peaks in the 30s to 40s and decreases with age. In men, the highest quartile of grip strength for both hands combined is 113 to 159 kg or 250 to 350 lb. That's in their 30s. And in women, 68 to 110 kg or 150 to 245 lb in their 40s. The strongest cortile of 70 yearear-old men have a grip strength of 79 to 110 kg or 175 to 245 lbs. And women 54 to 77 kg or 120 to 170 lb for both hands combined. You definitely don't want to be below the 75th percentile of your age group when it comes to grip strength because it means you're as strong as the average person, which is a very low standard. My last grip strength result showed my grip strength for both arms combined was 134 kg or 295 lbs. That puts me into the middle of the highest cortile for males in their 30s, which is my age group. Number three, HSCP. Inflammation is at the root of all diseases and it increases with age, which is a term called inflammaging. HSCP or highly sensitive C-reactive protein is a marker that assesses systemic inflammation. is one of the easiest and most common markers of inflammation. There are others, but as a single marker, HSCP can have great predictive value. HSCP levels are associated with increased all causeity and heart disease in a linear fashion. The higher the CRP, the higher the risk, and the optimal CRP levels are as close to zero as possible. A CRP of 1 to 3 mg per liter is linked to a 30% higher risk of all cause mortality and 43% higher risk for cardiovascular disease mortality. So, a healthy CRP should be below 0.5 mg per liter. My average CRP levels are around 0.1 to 0.2, which is virtually zero. But my latest test in March showed my CRP to be 0.01 mg per liter, which is barely detectable. Number four, blood pressure. High blood pressure is called a silent killer because it's slowly killing you and you can't feel it. You can't feel high blood pressure, but even slightly elevated blood pressure increases the risk of cardiovascular disease and neurodeeneration. Normal blood pressure for adults is between 100 to 130 for systolic and 60 to 80 for diastolic blood pressure. Ideally, it should be lower than 120 to 80 and closer to 110 to 70. You shouldn't measure your blood pressure once a year at the doctor's because it's not representative of your regular blood pressure. That's why it's useful to have a blood pressure monitor at home that you can use once a week or every other day if you want. Before measuring your blood pressure, you have to be sitting still and calm for 5 minutes without having consumed stimulants for the past few hours. Then you measure your blood pressure once your heart rate has decreased and you're not stimulated. My average blood pressure is 110 to 75. Number five, LP little A. One of the most aogenic lipoproteins is LP little A or lipoprotein A. LP little A is the strongest genetically determined aogenic lipoprotein which means that its levels vary a lot between individuals. They can vary a thousandfold ranging from close to zero to 300 mg per deciliter. LP little A below 50 mg per deciliter is considered normal but anything above 8 is already linked to a higher risk of heart disease. A 2021 large UK bioank study among 460,000 subjects discovered a linear increase in athoscerotic cardiovascular disease risk after an LP little A concentration of 8 mg per deciliter. Basically the higher the LP little A levels the higher the risk of developing heart disease. At the lowest risk is below 8 milligs per deciliter. At LP little A of 40 milligs per deciliter, the risk increases by 20%. at 100 milligs per deciliter by 50% and at 160 mgs per deciliter by up to 100%. My own LPA levels are around 2 milligs per deciliter which is pretty much as low risk as possible. You can control your LP little A levels slightly with medications and lifestyle but you can't control it that much. However, it's still good to measure your LP little A levels once to see where is your baseline. With that information, you can adjust your other risk factors accordingly. Number six, hemoglobin A1c. High blood sugar is similar to high blood pressure. You can't feel it, but it's killing you slowly. Glycated hemoglobin or hemoglobin A1c reflects your average blood sugar over the past few months. It's a good marker to know how much glycation and elevated blood sugar your body is experiencing. Diabetes begins with an hemoglobin A1c of 6.5% or higher. In terms of mortality risk, there's a linear association between hemoglobin A1c levels above 5.5% and primary cardiovascular events and mortality. The lowest all cause mortality has been observed within hemoglobin A1c below 5.2%. So you want your hemoglobin A1c to be at 5% or slightly lower, although there's no evidence that a score of 4.5% would be better. My average hemoglobin A1c is between 4.8 to 5%. Number seven, Cooper test. Having good cardiorespiratory fitness is associated with lower mortality and less heart disease. That's because to have good cardiorespiratory fitness, you need to do cardio, which is good for your heart and it lowers your blood pressure. Cardiores respiratory fitness is typically measured by looking at your V2 max or maximum oxygen consumption during exercise. A V2 max above 50 has been seen to be associated with the lowest mortality. One way to calculate your V2 max at home is to do the Cooper test. You basically run as far as possible within 12 minutes. The farther you run, the higher your V2 max will technically be. The lowest mortality risk of V2 max 50 would require you to run 2.75 km or 1.72 miles in 12 minutes. You can use online calculators like this to calculate your V2 max from your Cooper test result. The Cooper test isn't 100% accurate and it has some discrepancies with the standard V2 max test. For example, I've run 3.2 km of the Cooper test within 12 minutes which would give me a V2 max of 60, but I've seen greater scores on the actual V2 max test. So there are some discrepancies between there. However, as a free test of your card respirator fitness, the Cooper test is excellent. Keep in mind the same idea could be applied to 1 kilometer or one mile test. You could use those as well, but the main idea is the same. The faster you're able to run, the lower your mortality risk. All of those markers can be improved with proper lifestyle that incorporates different aspects of longevity. Check out my full evidence-based longevity routine

=== FILE: Microplastics in Your Body？ Eat This. [uxfWQFfUqWU].en.txt ===

You've probably heard that microplastics can mess with your fertility, hormones, and maybe even increase the risk of heart disease. But here's what almost nobody talks about. Their impact on your gut health. In 2023, a French study found the first direct evidence that microplastics damage your gut microbiota and weaken the intestinal barrier. When that barrier breaks down, these particles can slip into your bloodstream and travel to places you really don't want them to, like your brain, kidneys, or testicles. That's the bad news. But here's the good news. There's emerging research showing that certain probiotics and prebiotics can not only protect your gut from this damage, but actually help excrete microplastics from your body. In a 2023 study, male mice were exposed to microplastics and then given probiotics. What they found was that the probiotics reduced inflammation and restored the decline in sperm quality caused by the microplastics. So what kind of probiotic foods degrade these microplastics? Lactobacillus rotary you can get from fermented yogurt, cheese, pickles, tempeh and miso. Lactobacillus acidifilus you can get the most from yogurt and cafir but also sauerkraut and kombucha. Like the basilus plantarum is found in sauerkraut, pickles, sourdough bread and brined olives. If I were to sum it up, then eat more fermented foods.

=== FILE: Millions Take This Supplement — But It May Be Dangerous [P_jB8be-SuQ].en.txt ===

Most people think that supplements are harmless, just natural little boosters to your health. But here's the truth. Some supplements can actually be harmful for your health, or at least you should think twice before taking them. So, in this video, I'm going to go through these supplements. Number one, BCAAs. When I started to go to the gym more seriously around 12 years ago, the first supplement I ever took was branch chain amino acids or BCAAs. Why? Because they're marketed as amino acids that help you build more muscle. You take them in between meals when you're not eating to avoid muscle breakdown. The irony is that taking BCAAs alone can actually result in greater muscle breakdown. That's because BCAAs only contain three of the essential amino acids, leucine, isolucine, and valene. You need all nine of the essential amino acids to stimulate protein synthesis, and the three BCAs fall short of that. ingesting BCAAs alone has been seen to result in decreased muscle protein synthesis through reduced essential amino acid concentrations. The body gets the signal to increase protein synthesis from leucine, but because it doesn't have the other eight building blocks, it catabolizes its own tissue to get them. So, if you were to take BCAAs on an empty stomach without eating anything, you're probably going to break down more muscle than you're going to build. And if you take BCAAs with a meal or with a protein shake or something like that, then you're getting all the nine essential amino acids from the food that you're eating. So in that case, BCAAs are a waste of money. Clinical trials show that BCA supplementation has no effect on muscle growth or exercise performance. The most consistent benefit is the reduction in muscle soreness and creatine kynise after resistance exercise. BCA's also reduce the amount of tryptophan entering the brain because they compete with tryptophan uptake. This prevents the production of serotonin, the neurotransmitter of coldness. There's also a correlation between higher circulating BCA levels and insulin resistance, obesity, diabetes, and heart disease. Individuals with the highest BCA concentrations have a 2 to fivefold higher risk of developing diabetes. Now, I don't think that it's necessarily causal that higher BCA amounts would cause diabetes. It's just that during insulin resistance, you have abnormally high levels of BCAAs in the blood. However, clinical trials have shown that reducing BCA intake improves glucose tolerance, body composition, and insulin sensitivity in humans and mice. So, in the best case scenario, BCAAs are just a waste of money. But in the worst case scenario, BCAAs make you lose more muscle tissue if you take them in a faster state, and they might increase your risk of diabetes. Although, I think that risk would only apply to people who already have metabolic disease or insulin resistance, not healthy people. Number two is iron. Iron is an essential mineral and iron deficiency anemia is the most common nutrient deficiency in the world. Unfortunately, too much iron promotes atheroscerosis and heart disease because iron is easily oxidized and if you have too high iron levels in the blood, it begins damaging the blood vessels. High iron levels in the blood haven't been seemed to be associated with a high risk of heart disease and more vulnerable plaque in the arteries, which is the worst kind of plaque. There aren't any studies specifically looking at the effects of iron supplementation on heart disease risk or aththeroscerosis because you know it would be unethical to do that kind of a study. But the evidence around high iron status and increased risk of heart disease is quite consistent. The only people who would benefit from iron supplementation are people who have iron deficiency or heart failure. However, even a 2021 meta analysis of 10 studies saw that oral and introvenous iron supplementation didn't reduce mortality in iron deficient heart failure patients. So it all depends on your iron status. Normal iron levels are 70 to 175 micrograms per deciliter for adult males and 50 to 170 micrograms per deciliter for adult females. Iron status higher or lower than that appears to be associated with increased risk. Number three, calcium. Calcium supplements have been seen to increase the risk of heart disease by raising blood calcium levels too high which causes hypercalcemia. This results in more calcium being stored in the arteries leading to the progression of atheroscerosis. This 10-year follow-up study on older adults saw that dietary calcium wasn't associated with increased coronary artery calcification whereas calcium supplementation was associated with a 22% higher risk. Calcium supplements also increase the risk of arrhythmias or irregular heartbeat. So, it's the calcium supplements specifically that appear to be harmful, especially in larger doses over 1,000 milligs per day. People who might be fine with taking calcium are people who one have low calcium intake from diet. They usually don't eat dairy or enough leafy greens or two they have low calcium levels in the blood. So for them the calcium supplement won't cause hypercalcemia. The biggest risk comes from people who are eating a lot of calcium. They're supplementing a lot of calcium and they have high calcium levels in the blood. Diabetes also appears to increase the risk as this 2023 study saw calcium supplementation being associated with heart disease events in people with diabetes. Calcium supplements are often recommended for post-menopausal women to reduce the risk of hip fractures. However, even post-menopausal women might see increased risk of heart disease from calcium supplements. A 2021 meta analysis of 13 randomized control trials saw that calcium supplementation at a dose of a,000 milligrams a day increased the risk of heart disease by 15% in healthy post-menopausal women. So calcium supplements might not be the best option even for postmenopausal women. For this, something like calcium alpha ketoglutarate might be a more suitable option because number one, it's lower in calcium, so you're getting a safe amount of calcium. Two, calcium EKG supplementation has been seen to increase bone density in post-menopausal women. Whenever you're taking calcium or vitamin D for that matter, then you should combine it with vitamin K2 and magnesium to reduce the calcification. Number four, resuratrol. Reseratrol is thought to be a longevity supplement, but the evidence from animal studies is very mixed and the general consensus right now is that it's not a longevity supplement. In the interventions testing program, resuratrol didn't extend lifespan of genetically heterogeneous mice, which tends to support the idea that reseratrol isn't a longevity supplement. Even Glacosmith Klein that paid $720 million for reseratrol shut down the reseratrol and certuin program in 2013. They stopped trying to turn reseratrol into a product probably because they saw the writing on the wall. The only condition under which reseratrol extends lifespan is obesity and metabolic disease as shown by a 2006 study where mice were fed an insanely fattening diet. Interestingly, reseratrol does appear to improve inflammation and metabolic markers in humans with diabetes and obesity as shown by several human clinical trials. The reason you want to think twice about taking reseratrol is that it blunts the positive effects of exercise on cardiovascular health in humans. Exercise improves lipids and metabolic markers, but reseratrol appears to amilarate those effects. Reseratrol also lowers DHEA levels, but it doesn't affect testosterone and DHT. DHEA is a precursor to testosterone. So it might be an insignificant effect. So unless you are obese and you have diabetes, you don't really have anything to gain from reseratrol. Another reseratrol cousin molecule is called praistelbine. And this molecule has no evidence for life extension either. There's actually very little human research about praelbine and the research we do have suggests it actually increases LDL cholesterol. Number five, metformin. Now metformin isn't a supplement. It's a diabetes drug, but I think it's worthwhile to mention it because a lot of people are recreationally taking metformin for the sake of longevity. The evidence for metformin's longevity effects are also quite conflicting even in animal research and it doesn't appear to have longevity benefits for non-diabetic humans either. Because of that, it's important to be aware of the potential risks and side effects of metformin. Metformin has been seen to reduce VOMX and inhibit the mitochondrial adaptations to aerobic exercise. Exercise increases whole body insulin sensitivity and V2 max, but Metformin blunts that, meaning that you get lower V2X gains than if you were to not take Metformin. Metformin has been seen to reduce testosterone levels and counteract the increased testosterone you see from better blood sugar levels, not only in men, but also women. I'm not saying that Metformin is the worst medication out there, but it is a net negative for an otherwise healthy individual. Instead of metformin, there is another class of diabetes drugs called SGLD2 inhibitors that have been seen to extend lifespan in mice. They also lower blood sugar and improve kidney function. And they're also seen to reduce the risk of mortality in humans. They do that without lowering testosterone and by even increasing V2. HLD2 inhibitors, they have side effects. The biggest one being an increased risk of genital fungal infections, but they have fewer side effects overall than metformin. Finally, we have antioxidant supplements like vitamin E and vitamin A. A 2021 cockrine review of clinical trials saw that vitamin E, vitamin A, and beta carotene were possibly associated with increased mortality risk whereas vitamin C and selenium were not. I think this is something you don't really have to worry that much about because these studies find an extremely small increased risk, something like 1 to 3%. It's not something to ignore completely, but because it's very difficult to measure things like all cortality, the effects can be because of something else. So, I wouldn't really worry about taking vitamin E or vitamin A. I don't really think anyone really needs vitamin A or vitamin E supplementation to begin with. Interestingly, you don't see increased mortality risk from things like NAC, asexanthin, melatonin, or other antioxidant supplements. However, taking antioxidants like NAC at the wrong time might blunt the benefits of exercise such as muscle hypertrophy. So, just don't take antioxidants after exercise and don't take too many antioxidants for no reason. As you can see, some supplements are better than others. I think you should try to avoid supplements that don't have any proven benefits. They're kind of speculative and they have documented side effects that can even damage your health. And as far as we can tell, it's really important to the restoration of all bodily systems and for updating our models of how the world works. First, we have to talk about the importance of sleep. Practically all animal species have sleep-like behavior and there's little evidence of animals foregoing sleep without paying some health consequences. We spend nearly onethird of our lives being asleep and if we sleep less than that, we're probably going to live shorter. Here are some of the major side effects of not sleeping enough. Sleep loss and sleep disturbances shorten tie which suggests accelerated aging. Short sleep and insomnia have been found to be linked to accelerated epigenetic aging. Sleep deprivation accelerates skin aging and makes it more vulnerable to UV damage. People also report their own and other people's facial skin appearance looking worse after bad sleep. Poor sleep is linked with neurodeeneration and other ailments. During sleep, deep sleep especially, the brain's waste disposal system clears toxic substances from the brain. Therefore, a lack of deep sleep could predispose people to Alzheimer's. Short and bad sleep increases the risk of diabetes. People who sleep less than 5 hours have a 106% higher odds of pre-diabetes compared to those who sleep 7 hours. Just a single night of sleeping 5 hours reduces insulin sensitivity in healthy people. Short and bad sleep also increases the risk of heart disease. Sleeping less than 7 hours is associated with increased risk of heart disease. Sleep deprivation makes your body more susceptible to gaining weight due to increased calorie intake and reduced energy expenditure. a study a few years ago in which the researchers took all of these studies that had been done and what they found was that short sleep was associated with a 12% increased risk of death, a 37% increase in the risk of developing diabetes, 17% increase in risk of developing high blood pressure, 26% increase in risk of developing coronary heart disease and a 37% increased risk of developing obesity. Next, we have to talk about how much sleep is actually needed. The recommended amount of sleep is 7 to nine hours for most adults. Sleeping 7 to nine hours per night is associated with a reduced risk of coronary artery disease, stroke, and all cause mortality. It's been found that people who sleep less than 6 hours have increased risk of all cause and cardiovascular disease mortality. However, multiple studies have also found that sleeping over 9 hours is linked with increased mortality, diabetes, heart disease, and stroke. Often when people have found that long sleep is associated with worse health, that's because people who have worse health need more sleep to try and recover from whatever they're facing. We see this for example acutely in the case of infection. On average, I sleep about 7 to 8 hours per night, but sometimes 9 hours. And my heart rate variability ranges from 100 to 130, which is excellent and much higher than the average person. This all indicates that I'm getting sufficient amounts of quality sleep and I'm not lacking any recovery. Here are some of the main things I do to improve my sleep and get those scores. Number one, consistent bedtime and wake up time. Going to bed in the evening and waking up around the same time helps anchor your circadian rhythms. It improves sleep onset, overall sleep quality and recovery. Irregular sleeping patterns are associated with metabolic syndrome. Irregular sleepwig cycles will keep the body's circadian rhythms misaligned. Circadian rhythm misalignment is linked to various chronic diseases, including obesity. A 2021 UK bioank study on over 100,000 people found that sleep onset between 10 to 11:00 p.m. was associated with the lowest incidence of cardiovascular disease. Sleep onset between 11:00 p.m. to midnight was linked to 12% higher incidence of heart disease. Sleep onset after midnight with 25% higher incidence. I usually go to bed at 9:30 p.m. and I'm asleep by 10 p.m. And in the morning, I wake up around 6:00 to 7:00 a.m. Number two, avoid bright lights in the evening. Short wavelength light, which often looks blue, but is also present in white light and other cold colors, suppresses melatonin and can disrupt the circadian rhythms. Melatonin is not only important for sleep but also for antioxidant defense, anti-aging and managing inflammation. Exposure to light at night is linked with obesity, metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease, depression and cancer. Regarding light exposure and melatonin production, both the wavelength of the light and the intensity of the light are important. Short wavelength light, which is light that has a wavelength of roughly 480 nanometers, most potently activates the cells in the eye that trigger events leading to the suppression of melatonin synthesis and to many other so-called non-visual functions. And then the degree to which melatonin is suppressed depends on the intensity of light. So dimming the lights and using indirect sources of light is ideal if you need to see during the biological nighttime. And I therefore typically recommend that people dim the lights beginning about 3 hours before they plan to go to bed. === FILE: Not All Magnesium Is Created Equal (Here's Why) [nx8g0CeUzwU].en.txt ===

Magnesium is one of the most important minerals in your body and it's involved in over 300 processes starting with energy production and ending with brain function. Just look at this graph. But here's the problem. Most magnesium supplements don't actually reach the brain. This changed in 2010 when scientists at MIT created magnesium L38ate that could easily cross the bloodb brain barrier and it was seen to enhance learning and memory in rats. In mice with Alzheimer's disease, magnesium 30onate has been seen to improve memory and reduce synaptic loss, which could slow down neurodeeneration. That's cute. But what about humans? A 2022 randomized control trial in China saw that 30 days of supplementing with 2 g of magnesium L38 per day improved cognitive performance and memory. The effects were more pronounced in older participants than younger ones. Another 2015 clinical trial saw that magnesium 30onate improved working memory and executive functioning in older people with cognitive impairment. So there are two clinical trials showing that magnesium L3 specifically has benefits in cognition and memory. But these results are seen in people with cognitive impairment or older individuals who tend to have worse cognition because of aging. Magnesium is super important for the brain as it regulates neurotransmitters and energy production. Your brain uses 20% of your total body energy. So you need a lot of energy for the brain. Usually magnesium is attached to different salts like oxide, citrate or sulfate. But these have quite bad bioavailability and poor absorption and virtually none of them get into your brain. L38ate is a sugar acid which is a metabolite of vitamin C and it enhances magnesium's transportation across the bloodb brain barrier. === FILE: Omega-3 and Vitamin D Together Do Something Scientists Didn't Expect [L7duHL445Ck].en.txt ===

Omega-3s and vitamin D are two of the most popular supplements out there. Almost every doctor recommends them, but this year, two clinical trials tested whether supplementing omega-3s and vitamin D could slow down biological aging. I'm a big fan of vitamin D and omega-3s, but the takeaway isn't as simple as take this to live longer. In this video, I'm breaking down these new studies and discuss whether you should take these supplements to slow down aging on a cellular level. The first study was published in February 2025 and they analyzed the data of 777 participants of the do health clinical trial. The people took 2,000 IUs of vitamin D and or 1 gram a day of omega-3s and or follow a simple atome exercise program for over 3 years. They used four DNA methylation epigenetic clocks. Phenoage which estimates biological age based on mortality related biomarkers. Grimage 1 and Grimage 2 which predict biological age based on DNA methylation markers and Dun needed and pace that estimates the speed of biological aging. Omega-3s alone were seen to lower biological age clock scores. Pheno age by about 2.9 months lower, Grimage 2 by about 3.8 months lower and Dunadian pace around 1% slower speed of aging. People who had the lowest omega-3 status in the beginning of the study saw the greatest epigenetic reduction, which highlights the specific effects of raising omega-3 status. However, the effects on phenoage were greater when omega-3s were combined with vitamin D and exercise. Omega3 plus vitamin D around 3.5 months lower, omega3 plus exercise around 3.6 months lower, omega3 plus vitamin D plus exercise around 3.8 months lower, and vitamin D plus exercise around 3.5 months lower. Vitamin D and exercise alone had no significant individual effects on these clocks. But when vitamin D and exercise were combined, it did result in a 3.5 month lower pheno age score. These are quite interesting findings and I think most people would agree that omega-3s, vitamin D and exercise are good for your health. This study looked at the effects of these interventions on your health on an epigenetic level which further supports their health claims. The problem with these clocks is that as the researchers acknowledged, there's no gold standard or standardized measure of biological age. Each clock will give you different results, so you don't know which one is the accurate one. They chose these four specific clocks because they're the most clinically validated ones. But this doesn't mean that they're 100% accurate. My personal opinion is that you can't take the clocks at face value because based on these results, exercise would have no effect on biological aging. Yet, exercise has some of the most consistent research out there regarding health benefits. The second study was published in May 2025, and it looked at the effects of 2,000 IUs a day of vitamin D and 1 gram of omega-3s for 5 years. After 4 years, it was seen that vitamin D supplementation preserved tie length. Vitamin D slowed till shortening by about 140 base pairs compared to placebo. But omega-3s alone had no effect on tie length. TieRes are protective caps on top of chromosomes that protect your DNA. Tieamir shortening is one of the hallmarks of aging. With age, your tie get shorter. However, a lot of scientists agree that tieumirs aren't a reliable biomarker of aging. Having longer tie doesn't mean that you're going to live longer. Expressing tmease, the enzyme that grows tieumirs, is also implicated in cancer, and it's critical for the development of about 85% of human cancers. However, faster shortening of tie is associated with many chronic diseases such as diabetes, Alzheimer's, and heart disease. This doesn't mean that tie shortening causes these conditions, but it might be a side effect of the disease state. This particular study on vitamin D and omega-3 supplementation saw that vitamin D slowed down the decline and the shortening of tieamirs, which can be interpreted as a beneficial side effect of vitamin D supplementation. But we also need to look at the other studies done on omega-3s and vitamin D to make any conclusions about their health effects because the idea of biological aging clocks is a bit limited. Has vitamin D and omega-3s been seen to reduce the risk of chronic diseases and mortality? That's what we want to know. Regarding omega-3s, then the answer is an astounding yes. Two 2021 meta analysis of randomized control trials found that supplementation of EPA and DHA at a dose of 0.4 four to six grams a day was associated with a significant reduction in the risk of cardiovascular disease events and mioardial inffection in a dose dependent manner. Meaning that higher doses yielded greater results. Every additional gram per day was linked to an additional 9% reduction in the risk of myioardial inffection. Higher blood omega-3 levels are also associated with a lower risk of all cause mortality, Alzheimer's, and heart disease. Those with the highest levels of omega-3s have up to a 21% lower risk of all cause mortality compared to those with the lowest levels. To know if you're getting enough omega-3s, you need to measure your omega-3 index, which reflects the amount of EPA and DHA in your red blood cells. An optimal omega-3 index associated with the lowest mortality risk is above 8% and up to 12%. But above 6.5% is already acceptable, although not ideal. An omega-3 index below 4% put you in an increased risk category. So based on all the hundreds of clinical trials out there, omega-3 supplementation and having a higher blood omega-3 status is beneficial for reducing the risk of mortality, the risk of heart disease, Alzheimer's, and has a beneficial effect on a whole host of biomarkers. With vitamin D, it's a little bit more nuanced. There's no doubt that vitamin D deficiency is associated with a higher risk of all causality, cancer, heart disease, diabetes, dementia, and accelerated aging. But this applies to your blood vitamin D levels. The optimal blood vitamin D level is between 30 to 50 nanogs per milliliter or 75 to 125 nanomles per liter. If it's below that, it's a sign of insufficiency and above that it's possibly excessive. Using vitamin D supplements can raise your vitamin D status in the blood and there are also some benefits to supplements. But vitamin D supplements alone don't provide all the benefits of natural sunlight, specifically the UV and infrared radiation. However, it is reasonable to say that it's better to raise your blood vitamin D status artificially than be deficient in vitamin D. The studies about measuring biological aging were done on supplemental vitamin D, which indicates you can get some additional benefits from vitamin D supplementation beyond just raising blood vitamin D levels. Here's a list of things vitamin D supplementation has been shown to do in clinical trials. lower cholesterol and triglycerides, raise testosterone levels, raise glutathione levels, which is a powerful antioxidant, reduce the incidence of diabetes among those with vitamin D deficiency, decrease insulin resistance slightly. Here's a list of things vitamin D supplements have failed to do in clinical trials. Increase bone mineral density, improve depression, reduce blood pressure, improve multiple sclerosis, and cause weight loss. The clinical research about vitamin D supplementation isn't conclusive because there's a lot of difference in the dosing of vitamin D that's used in the studies and people also have a different baseline status of vitamin D. Vitamin D supplements will probably have a bigger effect on people who are deficient in vitamin D compared to those who are getting enough sunlight and they have normal vitamin D status. So the main goal would be to get your vitamin D status into the optimal range with or without supplements. That depends on the situation. All right, let me give an overview. Omega-3 supplementation has been shown to lower biological age scores based on several epigenetic age clocks. Most consistently the pheno age clock, which is based on 10 blood markers. So, it's technically not an epigenetic clock, just a blood marker clock. Combining omega-3 supplements with vitamin D supplements and exercise provides additional benefits to pheno age reduction. Vitamin D alone doesn't reduce biological age, but it appears to slow down tie shortening, which omega-3s don't. So, vitamin D and omega-3s appear to complement each other quite nicely. Omega-3s have a long history of other health benefits based on hundreds of clinical trials, such as a lower incidence of heart disease, diabetes, and Alzheimer's. Vitamin D has less evidence as a supplement, but maintaining optimal blood vitamin D levels should be a high priority for everyone. Keep your omega-3 index above 8% and your vitamin D levels between 30 to 50 nanogs per milliliter, which is 75 to 125 nanomles per liter. The problem is that most people never test it. So in this video, I'll explain what is homocysteine, what does it do, and how does it relate to a future risk of a stroke and heart attack. Homocysteine is a sulfur-containing amino acid produced from methionine, which is the most abundant amino acid in our diet, mostly coming from animal protein. In the body, homocysteine acts as an intermediate molecule that is either recycled back into methionine via folate and vitamin B12 or converted into cysteine via vitamin B6. High homocysteine levels are an independent risk factor for cardiovascular disease, myocardial infarction, hypertension, osteoporosis, neurodegeneration, thrombosis, and all-cause mortality. Not only is this association seen in observational studies, but genetic Mendelian randomization studies using variants such as MTHFR, C677T that raise homocysteine levels also find higher risk of cardiovascular disease, which supports the idea that the relationship may be causal rather than purely due to confounding. There's also mechanistic evidence to support it, because homocysteine damages the blood vessels, disrupts endothelial function, promotes arterial stiffness, promotes lipid peroxidation and oxidation of LDL, and it breaks down HDL, all of which promote atherosclerosis, thrombosis, and cardiovascular disease. In the context of a stroke, high homocysteine levels damage blood vessels and promote clot formation, which can cause a stroke. Clots break off from soft atherosclerotic plaque that forms oxidized LDL, endothelial dysfunction, and vascular inflammation, all of which high homocysteine promotes. Usually, strokes happen in people in their 60s and 70s. However, there are case reports of people in their late 20s who get an ischemic stroke and that had moderately elevated homocysteine, around 27 micromoles per liter. Now, not everyone with high homocysteine is going to get a stroke, but it is a causal risk factor. Most stroke patients with elevated homocysteine also have traditional risk factors, such as hypertension, diabetes, smoking, dyslipidemia. Homocysteine is rarely the only explanation for stroke. However, homocysteine is tested if no other risk factors are present, and a stroke occurs in a young person. So, homocysteine is a more useful test in younger people with no other risk factors. In younger people with no risk factors, they get a stroke, they usually have high homocysteine. The normal homocysteine range is 8 to 14 micromoles per liter for men and 6 to 12 micromoles per liter for women. Moderate hyperhomocysteine is characterized by 16 to 30 micromoles per liter. Intermediate is 31 to 100 and severe over 100. In people with premature gray hair who are younger than 20, B12 deficiency has been observed more frequently. === FILE: Protein Intake and Lifespan： What the Studies Show [xyEx56hrhL8].en.txt ===

Protein is the most controversial nutrient in longevity research. Too much protein is going to shorten your lifespan and give you cancer. Not enough protein will make you skinny and frail. No wonder most people are so confused. And to be honest, the scientists don't agree with each other either. The studies and protein are very mixed and conflicting. That's why in this video, I'm focusing only on the largest analysis on this topic, and I'll give you a few science-based rules of thumb that you can actually use. So, a lot of people say that protein is bad for your longevity, but is it really the case? This 2020 systematic review and meta analysis of 32 prospective studies on over 715,000 people found that higher protein intake was associated with a lower risk of all cause mortality with an intake of 14 to 23% of total calories as protein being linked to a lower risk. A protein intake over 25% was seen to be associated with a higher risk. That's not a low protein intake by any means. In fact, it's higher than the current recommended daily allowance of protein, which is around 10 to 15% of total calories. A protein intake of 14 to 24% on a regular 2,000 calorie diet is around 70 to 120 grams of protein, which is a decent amount. And it's higher than the 0.8 g per kilogram of RDA, which would give you 54 to 80 g of protein. So, the real world data doesn't support the idea that high protein intake is bad for your longevity. It's actually the opposite. I'm talking about a diet that consists of 10% protein versus a diet that is 15 to 25% protein. The study that I just mentioned, the absolute lowest risk was seen at 17 to 20% of total calories. That's nearly twice as much as the RDA. High protein diets are associated with reduced mortality, even more pronounced in the elderly people because they tend to be at a higher risk of frailty and malnutrition. A 2023 study saw that among people over 65, a protein intake of over 19.1% of total calories was associated with the lowest mortality risk. So, a diet that consists of around 20% protein is actually associated with the lowest mortality risk in all age groups, especially in the elderly people. Above 26% of total calories, you do start to see a small increase in mortality risk. But to be honest, we don't have solid data about that because there's not a lot of research about diets that consist over 26% of calories as protein. The first rule of longevity is to not take unnecessary risk. If there's no physiological requirement to eating more than 25% of your calories as protein, then why do it? The optimal amount of protein for muscle growth is 1.6 grams per kilogram per day or 0.74 g per pound, which has been shown in large meta analyses on the topic quite consistently. For most people, that's around 20% of calories coming from protein depending on their body weight. Interestingly, that matches the amount for lowest mortality risk. You can even build muscle on lower protein intake, as little as 1.2 g per kilogram. But the maximum results are observed at 1.6 grams per kilogram. Now, of course, some people will build more muscle by eating more protein. Other people build muscle by eating less protein. But generally speaking, there's no physiological requirement to eat more than 25% of your calories as protein. And based on the mortality studies, the sweet spot appears to be something like 17 to 20%. The reason why protein is thought to be bad for longevity is because of this thing called mtor or mamalian target of rapamy. MTOR is like a growth switch that makes things grow. muscles, brain cells, fat cells, but also cancer cells. Because of that reason, inhibiting mTor has been seen to extend lifespan in virtually all animal species that have been investigated, flies, mice, and yeast. In fact, suppressing mTor with the drug rapomy has a 60% increase in lifespan of middle-aged mice, which rivals the longest life extension of 65% seen in calorie restriction, which also partly suppresses mtor signaling. Now, we can't draw any conclusive answers from these mechanistic studies and animal research because the results might be completely different in humans, but it's undeniable that mTor is involved in aging. We just don't know how it relates to protein intake because there are a lot of other things that influence mTor activity. You clearly can't suppress mTor all the time because you're going to die to frailty and you might possibly increase the risk of dementia because you need mTor for growing brain cells. At the same time, chronic mtor activation increases the risk of cancer and it prevents the brain from clearing out these toxic proteins and amalite that accumulates during neurodeeneration. My opinion is that you want to cycle between activating mtor and suppressing mtor. You want to have periods of growth and you want to have periods of clearance where you clean out old junk material. That's why I love to do intermittent fasting. But there are other ways to achieve this. Another problem is that we don't know how much mtor is optimal for longevity because it's very hard to measure. One possible biomarker for mTor activity is IGF-1 or insulin like growth factor one that regulates growth and bone density. High IG of 1 levels are associated with increased risk of cancer, heart disease and mortality. But low IG of 1 is also implicated in mortality due to frailty and dementia. The lowest risk for cancer, cardiovascular disease and all cause mortality is seen at 120 to 160 nanogs per milliliter of IG of 1. Not too low but not too high. The interesting thing is that IG of 1 predicts longevity in centinarians which might mean that people with lower IG of1 levels due to genetics reach extremely old age. The key here is that we shouldn't focus on mTor per se because number one we can't measure it. Number two we don't know how much is too much and number three many things influence mTor not just protein. Carbohydrates do, saturated fat does, resistance training does, eating frequency and diabetes does so as well. Now I don't eat a low protein diet. I eat around 120 to 130 gram of protein which is 1.6 g per kilogram for me. In the past I used to eat a lot more like 160 180 g but despite that my IG1 levels have always been on the lower end around 100 and the reason for that in my opinion is in fasting. I eat one to two times per day and this keeps my IGF-1 levels low despite eating carbohydrates and despite eating protein. It might also be genetics but my theory is that it's intermittent fasting. All of this is to say that by focusing on mTor, we're focusing on the wrong things. We could focus on things like IG of 1 as a quasi marker of mTor expression and we do find a correlation between I of1 levels and mortality. But we also have to focus on other things related to longevity such as muscle mass, cognitive function, bone density, and muscle strength because if you're too low in IG of 1 and too low in mtor expression, you might increase the risk of frailty and dementia. Another relevant and highly conflictive topic is the difference between animal protein and plant protein. The large meta study of 32 studies I mentioned earlier saw that a higher proportion of calories from plant protein was associated with a lower mortality risk. The lowest mortality risk was seen at 7 to 11% of calories coming from plant protein, perhaps up to 12 to 15%, but this wasn't specifically studied. For animal protein, higher than 10% of calories was associated with increased mortality risk. However, an intake of 5 to 9% was associated with a lower risk. This is the general trend you see in most observational studies that higher plant protein intake and lower animal protein intake is associated with reduced mortality. Now it might be that plant proteins are lower in certain amino acids like methane and leucine that increase mtor expression and thus explain the reduced mortality risk. It might also be the higher fiber intake that improves metabolic health and cardiovascular health is not clear. And because these are observational studies, you can't completely tease out the other factors that influence the results, such as what else are you eating, what are you not eating, whether or not you exercise, how much you exercise, and what's your general lifestyle. In clinical trials, unprocessed red meat intake hasn't been seen to affect blood markers related to heart disease. So, you see quite inconsistent results from the randomized control trials. So, you can't make any definite conclusions based on these studies. Regarding maximum lifespan, then animal protein is high in methionine, which is an amino acid that's been seen to shorten lifespan in animals. Plant proteins are low in methane, whereas animal proteins are high in methane. However, if you get more glycine, then methane appears to be less harmful. It's just that most people are eating too much methane and they're not getting enough glycine, which might contribute to a shorter maximum lifespan. I like to always follow the precautionary principle. You don't want to take unnecessary risks and you want to er on the side of caution especially when we have conflicting data. That's why I think it makes sense to get more plant protein. But it doesn't look like being completely zero animal protein is necessary especially given that the meta analysis of 32 studies saw that an animal protein intake of around 5 to 9% of total calories was also associated with lower mortality risk and 7 to 10 12% of your total calories coming from plant protein was also associated with lower risk. I think that's a generally good pattern to aim for. All right, let me give an overview of how much protein you should eat. Getting around 15 to 23% of your calories from protein appears to be associated with the lowest mortality risk in large long-term human studies. That's around 70 to 150 g of protein for most people depending on their body weight and calorie intake. A much better number to aim for is the 1.6 g per kilogram or 0.74 g per pound as your maximum protein intake. Anything between 1.2 to 1.6 g per kilogram is also enough. For most people, that is going to end up being 17 to 23% of total calories as protein. We don't have evidence that protein intake over 25% of total calories is inherently harmful. But again, it's better to on the side of caution and not take unnecessary risks, especially if it's not going to increase your muscle hypertrophy if that's your goal. The biomarkers to monitor are IGF-1, muscle mass, muscle strength, cognition, and bone mineral density. If your muscle mass and bone density are low, you're at a higher risk of frailty and you need to do resistance training and increase your protein intake. If you have low IGF-1 levels, but your muscle and bone density is high, you don't have nothing to worry about. If you're eating only plant proteins, you might need a bit more protein. I would say 20% more than if you were to be eating only animal protein. So, instead of 70 to 150 g, you would eat 80 to 180 g depending on your body weight. It's important to realize that diet is only one single component of health. There are many other factors that are equally as important, if not even more important.

There have been several interesting papers over the last few years pointing out that there's a strong link between the circadian rhythms and aging. What are these circadian rhythms? Circadian rhythms are your body's natural day and night cycles that repeat roughly every 24 hours. It's basically your body's internal clock that regulates your hormones, body temperature, energy levels, strength, and even blood pressure. For example, natural testosterone production peaks in the morning around 9:00 a.m., whereas your body temperature is the highest in the evening at around 6:00 to 7:00 p.m. The way aging comes into play is by blunting the fluctuation in these hormones. Younger people maintain robustness and beak swings in their circadian rhythms. They produce a lot of cortisol in the morning, which is supposed to wake you up and energize you for the day. and they also produce a lot of melatonin in the evening to support sleep. Older individuals on the other hand have lower fluctuations in cortisol, melatonin, and body temperature. Their circadian rhythm is more flatlined. This graph illustrates it very nicely. You can see that adults produce a lot of melatonin and a lot of cortisol at the right times of the day. But for older people, it's nearly a complete flatline. I call this the chronic jet lag syndrome. Your body doesn't know what time of the day it is because there's no swings in these hormones. These fluctuations in hormones tell your body what time of the day it is and control all other hormones and other processes inside the body. As a result of that, all the people sleep worse. They sleep shorter. They have poorer inflammation status. They have poorer metabolic health and lower energy levels. As a result of that chronic circadian disruption and chronic jet lag, your body experiences higher DNA damage and higher inflammation. There's overwhelming amount of research showing that circadian rhythm disruption increases the risk of neurodeeneration, cancer, diabetes, obesity, hypertension, and heart disease. Every function, every process, every metabolic pathway, every hormone is regulated by the circadian rhythms. If your circadian clocks are working properly, your body works like clockwork. If the clocks are misaligned, your body goes through higher amounts of stress and a greater requirement for repair that accelerates aging. Number three, entrainment or receiving the cues from the environment that regulate circadian rhythms such as light, movement, food, and electromagnetic fields. All of these factors influence other hallmarks of aging and also the hallmarks of cancer. It looks like honey, it tastes like honey, but it's actually syrup. How do you know which honey is real and which one is fake? So, how serious is it? How much fake honey is out there? In 2018, the Canadian Food Inspection Agency tested 240 honey samples and found that 21.7% of them were adulterated. In Australia, 27% of honey brands were also fake. But in the US, it's estimated to be up to 70%. A 2023 report by the European Commission found that 46% of the 147 honey samples tested were adulterated and mixed with other syrups. 74% of honey from China was adulterated and 93% of honey from Turkey was adulterated. Then that Chinese honey in Thailand is sold to the EU and the US. The label on the bottle will say honey from Thailand, but in reality is from China. By doing that, they avoid hundreds of millions of dollars in shipping duties. So, one immediate tip here is to buy honey from your local beekeepers that can't hide behind international shell companies or hop borders, and they're less likely to sell you honey that's 50% corn syrup. There are also some methods used by researchers to detect adulterated honey. They involve more advanced light analysis and DNA barcoding. Unfortunately, these professional testing methods aren't possible at your home and you can't just do it. There are also some at home honey testing kits, but experts don't really recommend them because they're not very accurate. So, the only reliable method is to buy honey from your local beekeepers from your own country or your local state. Honey from regions with more regulations, such as Canada, the US, and the European Union or Australia is also generally pure, whereas honey from China, Turkey, Iran, etc. is more than likely mixed with other syrups. These countries are also able to produce honey very cheap, which drives your local beekeepers out of business. If the production cost for you is $2, but it's 10 cents for them, then you just can't compete even in your local market. So, even if the local honey is more expensive, it's worth it to support your local businesses, and you're going to be more certain that you're getting actual honey, not syrup. There are some other ways to detect fake honey. Read the labels. You'd be surprised to know that some honey bottles blatantly say that they're 50% syrup. Honey can crystallize and become solid, especially in the fridge. If your honey stays liquid like caramel, then it's probably syrup. Honey is also less sticky and more like a balm, whereas syrup is more gooey and sticky. Honey has a richer and more unique flavor, whereas syrup tastes like sugar. === FILE: The #1 Predictor of Longevity Nobody Trains Enough [bJo8V-YI6e8].en.txt ===

A lot of people who get into health and longevity start taking some supplements. They go to the gym a few times a week and they clean up their diet. Those are all very important cornerstones that you should focus on. However, there's one thing in research that over and over again seems to topple all these other factors, especially after the age of 20. I'm talking about cardiorespiratory fitness. The data is remarkably clear. Fitter people live longer. They have lower risk of heart disease, dementia, diabetes, and lower all cause mortality. In fact, if you ate a fairly average diet, slept reasonably well, and did nothing except regular cardio, you'd likely be healthier and live longer than someone with a perfect diet and supplement stack who doesn't exercise. It's that powerful. And in this video, I'm going to prove it. I'll also tell you how to get into good card fitness for the sake of longevity. The reason cardiorespirator fitness matters so much is because it's the earliest marker of physical fitness that starts declining. Cardiorestor fitness as measured by our max peaks in your early 20s and starts declining by about 10% per decade. This is based on the general population who doesn't exercise but it's relevant to everyone because if you don't train cardio, your V2 max is expected to drop in a similar pattern. V2 max refers to your body's ability to consume oxygen during exercise. The more oxygen your body is able to consume and utilize, the better your lungs, muscle, and heart are working. This decline in V2X is more so a sign of declining heart and lung function rather than a decline in fitness. The loss of fitness is the byproduct of declining organ function. And to keep your organs working more youthful, you need to train them. The only way to train them is to put them through exercise. A 2018 randomized control trial showed exactly that following a protocol of high-intensity exercise was able to make the heart of people in their mid-50s look and function like that of a 30-year-old. Their resting heart rate dropped, their ROMAX increased, and their myioardial stiffness also decreased. The reason I say cardioresive fitness matters more than any diet or supplement is because of the data. A higher card fitness has been consistently been shown to be associated with lower rates of heart disease, dementia, diabetes, and mortality. And I'm not talking about some small differences like you see with diet. The difference in high and low card fitness in terms of mortality risk is four-fold, which is 300%. That's more than any association with diet quality, and it rivals obesity and smoking. People with a V2 max of 50 have a four-fold lower mortality risk than those with a V2 max of 16.45. And the risk reduction is linear. The higher the V2 max, the lower the mortality. We don't have enough data about people with a V2 max of 60 and above, but a V2 max of 50 is relatively fit, although it's not very athletic. There was also a recent study from Norway that found that being unfit was worse for your survival than moderate alcohol consumption. The best case scenario is you always abstain from alcohol and you're always fit. But the groups that were fit and drank alcohol had a better survival than the groups who were unfit but avoided alcohol. It means that whatever the harmful effect of alcohol is, being unfit and not exercising is worse. The reason you want to train your cardio fitness and keep it high throughout your life is that you will stay healthier for longer than someone who experiences a faster decline in their fitness. There's a certain threshold of V2 max as well as muscle strength below which you dip into the frailty and immobility realm. there you'll have a hard time doing everyday activities such as walking, groceries, putting on clothes, and wiping your own butt. So, how do you go about increasing your cardio fitness? Well, the easy answer is you just do more aerobic exercise. There are many training methods you can use. You can do speed walking. You can do incline walking. You can do weighted vest walking. You can do zone 2 running, zone 2 cycling, swimming, high-intensity interval training, Tabata intervals, sprint intervals, 4x4 Norwegian protocol. The list goes on and on. The most important thing is to do aerobic exercise that elevates your heart rate for a prolonged period of time. And it doesn't have to be just running or cycling. You can see improvements in your cardio fitness and V2 max by doing weightlifting as well. However, there's a caveat here. The V2 max increasing effects of resistance training are limited to people who have a lower V2 max at the baseline. This 2013 review saw that only three out of 17 studies on younger individuals saw an increase in VMAX from resistance training. In older adults, it was six out of nine studies. The results also depended on baseline V2 max with resistance training giving significant benefits if the V2 max was below 40 in younger individuals and below 25 in older adults. So young and fit people don't really see significant V2 max gains from resistance training, but old unfit individuals do. That's why it's recommended to do some specific aerobic exercise. Here are some recommendations. Walking around 8,000 to 12,000 steps a day. It's great low impact, low inensity movement that's not going to be the make or break for your card regular fitness. However, it's low stimulus, low recovery, and longer duration. Once a week, you should do some high-intensity interval training, whether that be the 4x4 Norwegian protocol or anything else like that. You want to get your heart rate up to 80 to 90% of your maximum heart rate for at least 2 to 4 minutes in total for around 2 to four rounds. That's enough to get your V to max higher and to prevent age related decline. once or twice a week. Zone two cardio at 60 to 70% of your maximum heart rate for about 45 to 90 minutes. This is low intensity. You can do it while breathing through the nose. Zone 2 builds your aerobic base, which is important over the course of decades. The most important thing to maintain your card fitness is to train it. It's seen that even if you're athletic and fit in your youth, once you stop exercising, your card respiratory fitness goes down and in the process you lose all the benefits. In this study on elite athletes followed up for 22 years, those who completely stopped exercising saw a 15% decline in their V2 max over the course of a decade. Those who engaged in only weekend exercise saw a 10% decline, but those who kept running regularly saw only a 6% decline. 6% is still 6%, but compare it to 15% by not exercising at all. It's more than twice the amount of decline. If there's only one thing you do for your health without changing your diet, without changing your sleep, without changing your general exercise routine, then training your cardiorespiratory fitness is by far one of the most powerful things to extend your longevity and reduce the risk of chronic diseases. Here's the key difference. Sunlight is balanced. The mix changes throughout the day. Sunrise and sunset give you more red and amber tones, while midday has more blue light. === FILE: The Exercise That Made Hearts 20 Years Younger [Den_IVSV6AU].en.txt ===

What if I told you your heart has an age and you can make it younger? An aging heart becomes stiffer, pumps less efficiently, and loses its ability to respond to stress. Your max heart rate drops, stroke volume decreases, and the blood vessels stiffen. But here's the exciting part. Scientists have discovered a workout that can make your heart up to 20 years younger. It sounds too good to be true, but it's true. A 2018 randomized control trial took 60 healthy, sedentary middle-aged people in their 50s, and they were randomly assigned to either two years of structured exercise training or a control group. Those who exercised saw significant improvements in their VOMX, their fitness, and overall heart functioning. Effective arterial elastance reduced from 2.37 to 2.16. Arterial compliance increased from 1.07 to 1.29. stroke volume improved and plasma volume and hemoglobin also improved. Now, the MVP of this study was the 4x4 Norwegian protocol, but arguably other forms of high-intensity interval training can be equally as effective. It's just that this 4x4 protocol is very commonly known and is also brutally effective.

=== FILE: The Longevity Drug Scientists Are Excited About (Not Rapamycin) [Ui_nDiiE8Mo].en.txt ===

One of the pharmaceuticals that show promise in being beneficial for longevity in humans are SGLT2 inhibitors. SGLT2 or sodium glucose coransporter 2 inhibitors are diabetes drugs that work by blocking glucose reabsorption by the kidneys resulting in lower blood sugar and diuretic effects. However, SGLT2 inhibitor longevity benefits appear to be beyond just lowering blood sugar because metformin has failed to be associated with longevity in humans although it also lowers blood sugar. In this video, I'm going to look at into the research of SDLT2 inhibitors and why they might be beneficial for longevity. I'll also cover metformin. Subscribe for the latest updates in anti-aging research. Let's start with the 2024 study on half a million UK individuals that analyze the effects of 406 medications of mortality. Most drugs were associated with increased mortality because people who take drugs have some diseases that kill them. However, there were a few drugs associated with reduced mortality and SGLD2 inhibitors were number one with a 36% lower association with mortality. Interestingly, although metformin is also a diabetes drug and it lowers blood sugar, it had no effect on mortality. Metformin has this aura that it's a longevity drug and it will also make non-diabetics live longer. But the evidence doesn't suggest it at all. In 2014, an observational study suggested that diabetics taking metformin could live 15% longer than non-diabetics not taking metformin. But a recent 2022 reassessment of that 2014 study found that in case control pairs, using metformin was associated with increased mortality across all levels of cumulative use. Metformin use among diabetics does reduce all cause mortality and heart disease events, but not in non-diabetics. What about SGLT2 inhibitors? SGLD2 inhibitors lower long-term mortality in diabetics with or without kidney disease and irrespective of GLP-1 agonists. However, a 2022 meta analysis of 12 randomized control trials saw that SGLD2 inhibitors reduced cardiovascular mortality in diabetic patients with heart failure. In non-diabetics, they reduced the risk of hospitalization for heart failure without effects on cardiovascular mortality and stroke. Another 2021 meta analysis of randomized control trials saw that SGLD2 inhibitors improve cardiovascular outcomes in patients without diabetes with heart failure. They also showed positive metabolic outcomes in weight and blood pressure. Obviously, we don't have long-term randomiz control trials on healthy non-diabetic individuals taking SGL2 inhibitors. But SLD2 inhibitors appear to lower mortality in heart failure patients and diabetics. In people without diabetes, they improve metabolic health and reduce cardiovascular risk. However, in the interventions testing program, which tests the lifespan effects of molecules on mice, one of the SGL2 inhibitors, canaglosin, was seen to extend median survival of male mice by 14% and 90th percentile survival by 9%. The ITP is considered the gold standard program for testing the life extension effects of different molecules in mice. Metformin, on the other hand, was not seen to extend mouse lifespan in the ITP. It did so only when combined with rapamy. So based on animal and human research, metformin has no effects on lifespan. It will reduce the risk of mortality in diabetics, but diabetics have a shorter lifespan to begin with. SGLT2 inhibitors on the other hand do extend lifespan in mice, but we don't have evidence from non-diabetic humans yet. Out of SGL2 inhibitors and metformin, SGLD2 inhibitors have a lot more potential. There's a difference in metformin and SGLD2 inhibitors. Metformin decreases glucose production by the liver and increases insulin sensitivity. SGLD2 inhibitors on the other hand block glucose reabsorption in the kidneys and you excrete more glucose in urine. There are several other systemic effects that happen with SGL2 inhibitors. They also stimulate several longevity pathways like AMPK, PGC1 alpha, autophagy and lower mTor signaling. Now metformin does the same things. So the reason why SGLD2 inhibitors appear to provide a greater mortality risk than metformin is because SGLD2 inhibitors have systemic effects on the kidneys and heart whereas metformin is mostly lowering blood sugar. And just lowering blood sugar doesn't appear to be enough. The biggest downside to SLD2 inhibitors is their cost. They cost around $400 a month which is significantly more expensive compared to the $20 a month of metformin. The most commonly prescribed SGL2 inhibitors include canagylosin, depaglyphlosin, empaglyphlosin, and eruglyloin. You need a prescription for all of these. Now, pharmaceuticals often have side effects, which is why it's not a smart idea to just start taking them as a healthy person. Metformin, for example, has been seen to reduce V2X and testosterone levels, which are also important for longevity. Metformin also inhibits the mitochondrial adaptations to aerobic exercise. So, that's quite bad for an otherwise healthy person. SGL2 inhibitors on the other hand have been found to be associated with a small increase in peak V2 which is the opposite of metformin. However, this has been seen in patients of chronic heart failure. So, we don't know what's the effects in otherwise healthy people. In healthy men, SLD2 inhibitors haven't been seen to affect testosterone levels either. All of this suggests that SLD2 inhibitors have much fewer side effects on health span than metformin. However, SL2 inhibitors still have some side effects such as genital and urinary tract infections, nausea, fatigue, increased urination, dehydration, and potential low blood pressure or risk of amputation. SDL2 inhibitors are associated with a three to five-fold increased risk of fungal genital infections. So, you got to be careful with that and it might not be suitable for immunompromised individuals. At the end of the day, it's too early to say if SGL2 inhibitors are going to extend lifespan in humans, especially those who don't have diabetes. I think people who are younger than 50 years old and otherwise healthy, they kind of don't need to start taking SLD2 inhibitors or other blood sugar medications. They're already healthy and they're not that old that their blood sugar levels would be compromised. However, at older age above 60 and 70, your blood sugar and kidney function will already begin to decline. So, what's quote unquote normal for a 70-year-old can be categorized as pre-diabetes or early stage kidney disease in your 20s or 30s. Maybe at the age of 70 or above, you could benefit from SGL2 inhibitors. But you need to discuss these things with your doctor. Regardless, SGLD2 inhibitors show promise for being gerrotective and with longevity benefits, at least based on observational studies and animal studies. We just need more long-term studies to see if there are any long-term harmful side effects. Pharmaceuticals can be useful for some people, but you also need to have your lifestyle optimized.

=== FILE: The Muscle-Saving Supplement Nobody's Talking About [h6Mn-KfT2no].en.txt ===

HMBB is a supplement that's seen quite a lot of resurgence in popularity because it might help to build muscle and strength. However, there are some people saying that HMBB can actually replace exercise or that you need to exercise less while taking HMBB. In this video, I'm going to break down what does the research actually say about HMBB and whether or not you should supplement it. HMBB or beta hydroxy beta methylate is a byproduct of the amino acid leucine. Leucine is the key amino acid responsible for muscle protein synthesis that builds muscle. You need a specific amount of leucine, which for most people is 2.5 to three grams, to trigger muscle protein synthesis. However, the metabolism of leucine creates HMBB, which might also have effects on reducing protein breakdown. There is research that taking HMBB before exercise blunts the rise in muscle damage and protein breakdown from exercise, even in trained individuals. HMBB before resistance training appears to result in lower cortisol and higher testosterone after the training than placebo, which means the body experiences less wear and tear from exercise thanks to HMBB's anti catabolic effects. HMBB also stimulates muscle protein synthesis, which means you're more likely to be in a net positive anabolic state, resulting in more muscle. All of this would indicate that HMBB is amazing for muscle growth. You would build more muscle while taking HMBB, with all things being equal. But this is where things get a bit more controversial. In the early 2010s, there were several studies published by Dr. Wilson and colleagues that showed that supplementing HMBB resulted in greater increases in muscle mass and loss of fat mass compared to injecting testosterone. That's just bonkers. An over-the-counter supplement outperforming steroids. The results of these studies were taken with a lot of skepticism by the scientific lifting community. And nobody really thinks that HMBB is better than steroids. So, there was probably some sort of shenanigans going on with these studies. However, it doesn't mean that HMBB is useless or that it wouldn't help with muscle growth. Supplementing HMBB has been seen to increase muscle mass and strength in untrained and elderly people, but the effects are much smaller in already trained and advanced trainees. A 2020 meta analysis of 11 randomized control trials on 18 to 45 year olds saw that supplementing 3 g a day of HMBB didn't result in greater lean mass or strength compared to placebo. HMBB was seen to have some benefits in people eating less than 1.6 6 g per kilogram of protein, which is still more than what average people consume. What it means is that HMBB makes up for suboptimal protein intake because if you were on a high protein intake, you would get adequate amounts of HMBB from your diet. There is also an age related effect of HMBB with older individuals seeing greater benefits than younger individuals. A 2025 meta analysis of 21 randomized control trials on adults over the age of 50 saw significant improvements in muscle mass, strength, and gate speed from taking 3 grams a day of HMBB for at least 12 weeks. Doses below 3 g and shorter than 12 weeks were less effective. What's been consistently found is that HMBB supplementation reduces muscle wasting in older individuals. This makes HMBB a potential therapeutic option for sarcopenia and other conditions of frailty. With age, you see a decline in muscle mass and muscle strength starting in your mid-30s already. Let's be honest, most of this decline is because of disuse, not lifting weights. But it's also driven by aging. As you get older, your body becomes less sensitive to the muscle growth effects of eating protein. That's why a young person needs only 2.5 g of leucine to trigger muscle protein synthesis, but a person in their 80s might need twice that amount. Older people need more protein to maintain the same amount of muscle, not to mention build it. Supplementing HMBB is a way to achieve a more positive anabolic state. You trigger more protein synthesis than you break down. This can help you to maintain muscle on a lower protein intake. And for all the people who struggle to build muscle, it will also help to maintain that muscle. You should still lift weights and eat enough protein. But adding HMBB to the mix can help those who struggle with frailty or sarcopenia. I actually used H&M for several years myself and indeed notice some benefits. Now, you might wonder why? Because I'm not old. I don't have low muscle mass. I don't eat a low protein diet. So why did I take it? Well, I took it because I saw some of the studies and I thought it might help me to also build more muscle. However, my situation was a bit more special because I was also doing one meal a day intermittent fasting and I was taking HMBB in the morning in a fast state. Fasting is a state characterized by higher muscle protein breakdown and taking HMBB apparently reduces that resulting in a higher positive protein balance. So whenever I take HMBB, I do notice much better muscle retention and muscle growth because of that reason. probably if I were to eat three, four, five meals a day with protein, then I probably wouldn't see that effect. All right, let me give you a summary. Should you take HMBB? HMBB reduces muscle protein breakdown and has been seen to increase muscle mass and strength under specific conditions. Number one, you're eating a sub-optimal protein intake, which is less than 1.6 g per kilogram per day. Number two, you're experiencing muscle wasting due to some medical condition or just aging. Number three, you're a beginner to lifting weights. And number four, you're over the age of 50, especially over the age of 80. HMBB does reduce muscle breakdown and it can accelerate recovery even for trained individuals, but it's not going to result in significant gains if you eat high protein and you're lifting weights. The best time to take HMBB is either in a fast state or before exercise, and the optimal dose is 1.5 to 3 g a day. There are two types of HMBB, HMBB calcium and HMBB free acid. HMBB calcium has about 13% calcium. So 3 grams would provide 400 milligs of calcium which is a significant amount and it can be harmful for cardiovascular health. However, HMBB free acid is faster acting and it's cleared faster. So you should only take it before exercise whereas HMBB calcium can be taken in the fastest state without exercise. Overall I do think that HMBB is useful especially for the elderly people or those who are suffering from malnutrition frailty or psychopenia or maybe if you're doing some sort of extended inverted fasting.
