=== FILE: The Probiotic Hack to Get Microplastics Out of Your System [txn7p9xRfvc].en.txt ===

You've probably heard that microplastics can mess with your fertility, hormones, and maybe even increase the risk of heart disease. But here's what almost nobody talks about. Their impact on your gut health. In 2023, a French study in the Journal of Hazardous Materials found the first direct evidence that microplastics damage your gut microbiota and weaken the intestinal barrier. When that barrier breaks down, these particles can slip into your bloodstream and travel to places you really don't want them to, like your brain, kidneys, or testicles. That's the bad news. But here's the good news. There's emerging research showing that certain probiotics and prebiotics can not only protect your gut from this damage, but actually help excrete microplastics from your body. In this video, I'm walking you through these exact strains of bacteria backed by science. Exposure to microplastics has been seen to disrupt the gut microbiome by increasing harmful bacteria like helioacttorbilis and claustrdium coccleome. They also decrease beneficial bacteria like claustrodialis, bacteriodialis and recinelacea. This shift in the microbiome alters metabolites leading to immune dysregulation and inflammation. As a result, you have negative effects on male and female reproductive organs and the brain. A 2021 study from China also found that people with irritable bowel disease had a higher amount of microplastics in their stool. What it means is that people with IBD either eat a lot more foods that contain microplastics or the microplastics mechanistically promote the development of gut problems, including IBD. One of the most common gut health foods you hear about are probiotic fermented foods. There are studies finding that certain bacterial strains found in fermented foods can degrade chemicals in plastic products such as BPA. In a 2023 study, male mice were exposed to microplastics and then given probiotics. What they found was that the probiotics reduced inflammation and restored the decline in sperm quality caused by the microplastics. A 2025 study saw that giving mice the probiotic strains lactic acidbasillus parasf DT66 and lactyliplantibbacillus plantarum DT88 increased polisterine excretion by 34% and reduced residual polisterine particles in the intestine by 67%. That's massive. So what kind of probiotic foods degrade these microplastics? I'm going to give you the list of the ones that have been researched. Lactobacillus roery you can get from fermented yogurt, cheese, pickles, tempeh and miso. Lactobacillus acidifilus you can get the most from yogurt and cafir but also sauerkraut and kombucha. Lactobacillus plantarum is found in sauerkraut, pickles, sourdough bread and brined olives. There are also other foods with similar benefits. Anthocyanins found in blueberries and fruit aren't probiotics, but they're also investigated as potential options for mitigating microplastic induced toxicity. Inolin and betaglucans found in oats have also been shown to reduce the amount of forever chemicals called pifas in mice. To address the intestinal inflammation and permeability, you can also supplement glutamine because it's the amino acid that maintains tight junction and intestinal permeability. A 2024 meta analysis of clinical trials saw that 30 grams of glutamine a day for less than two weeks was able to reduce intestinal permeability. With less intestinal permeability, fewer microplastics get into the bloodstream. If I were to sum it up, then eat more fermented foods like cafir, yogurt, sauerkraut, pickles, miso, tempeh, and kimchi. You also want to incorporate colorful pigments that contain anthocyanins like blueberries. Some individuals with food sensitivities and gut problems might not react well to fermented foods. Fermented foods contain a lot of histamine because they're aged, which can cause allergy- like symptoms. Histamine intolerance arises primarily from a deficiency in the enzyme called diamine oxidase, DAO, that breaks down histamine, which can be supplemented if necessary. You can get histamine from not only fermented foods, but also processed meat, alcohol, and just food that's been sitting in the fridge for too many days. If you are sensitive to histamine, then you might not do well with fermented foods. But you can still contain the other foods that help with microplastics, namely the colorful fruits and vegetables like sweet potatoes, blueberries, and oats. All right, let me give you more tips for reducing the burden of microplastics on your body. Minimize plastics in your life. Replace plastic bottles and plastic Tupperware with glass bottles and glass boxes. Some foods also contain more microplastics because of being stored in a plastic container. Canned fish, canned fruit, canned vegetables, they all contain microplastics because of the plastic coating on the tin. But meat and fish stored in plastic wrappers have also been seen to contain millions of microplastics. So you want to try to opt for either frozen food or minimize the one wrapped in plastic. === FILE: The Real Reason Japanese People Live Longer [__Zuq6cVrVE].en.txt ===

Japanese people are one of the longest living people in the world with a life expectancy of 85 years. They also have the most centinarians in the world with over 120k people over the age of 100 making up 0.1% of their entire population. That's two to three times more than other countries. Now, there are many reasons why the Japanese live longer than others. They have healthier culture, smaller portion sizes, they walk more, they eat a little bit less processed food, they're less obese, they smoke less, they exercise more regularly, and they have good healthcare. However, there's one specific thing that sets Japan apart from other countries, and it could also explain the reason why they have lower rates of chronic diseases and lower risk of mortality. The reason is their exceptionally high omega-3 index, which reflects the amount of omega-3 fatty acids in their blood. Japanese people have an omega-3 index of over 8% whereas it's less than 4% in the USA and Canada and 4 to 6% in France and Spain. The Japanese diet is very rich in seafood, fish, crab, shrimp, as well as sea vegetables and seamos. These foods are high in omega-3 fatty acids that have a consistent and long track record of health benefits. I think we've all heard that omega-3 fatty acids are good for you. And the Japanese people are a prime example of that and they prove it with their blood work. The omega-3 index reflects the amount of omega-3 fats, DHA, and EPA, in your red blood cells that you can measure with a blood test. It's a long-term marker of your intake of omega-3 fats, whether from food sources such as fish, seafood, or sea vegetables, or omega-3 supplements. There's consistent research linking a higher omega-3 status with lower rates of heart disease, lower dementia, and lower risk of mortality. A 2021 meta analysis of 17 studies saw that people with the highest omega-3 index over 7.55% had a 15 to 18% lower risk of total mortality. A 2022 study also found that the risk of Alzheimer's disease among the highest red blood cell DHA quentile over 6.1% was 49% lower compared to the lowest quintile less than 3.8% in fully adjusted models. The omega-3 index associated with the lowest risk of heart disease mortality is over 8% whereas an index of less than 4% is linked to the greatest risk. So what is a good omega-3 index to have? Based on the research, an omega-3 index of 6 to 8% is already seem to be associated with a slightly lower risk of dying than an omega-3 index of 4% or lower than that. However, having an omega-3 index of 8% or higher appears to be even better. The benefits keep increasing until 11% after which they seem to plateau. But 11% is better than 8%, 8% is better than 6% and 6% is better than 4%. As I shared with you in the beginning of the video, Japanese people have an omega-3 index of over 8% as do the South Koreans. Americans are below 4% and Europeans are between 4 to 8% depending on the country. This works pretty parallel to the consumption of seafood in these regions. Americans eat the least seafood and Japanese and South Koreans eat the most seafood. There are also some regions with a very high omega-3 index such as Alaska and Greenland. But these regions tend to have poor health care and other co-orbidities that shorten their life expectancy compared to regions like Japan or South Korea. Now that we know these omega-3 fats are good for you, the next question is why? Why is it so? The reason has to do with how omega-3 fatty acids lower inflammation and improve metabolic health. A 2024 meta analysis of clinical trials found that omega-3 supplementation improves heart function, reduces inflammation, and decreases the risk of cardiovascular disease in patients with heart failure. On top of that, a 2020 meta analysis of 26 randomiz control trials concluded that omega-3s might improve insulin sensitivity and lipid metabolism in type 2 diabetics. Two 2021 meta analyses of randomized control trials found that supplementation of EPA and DHA at a dose of 0.4 four to six grams a day was associated with a significant reduction in the risk of cardiovascular disease events and myioardial inffion in a dose dependent manner. So having more omega-3 fats in your blood means you'll have lower inflammation, better endothelial function, better insulin sensitivity, and better lipid metabolism. All of this translates to lower risk of heart disease, dementia, and lower risk of mortality. Having a higher omega-3 index is a biomarker that you pretty much want to maintain for the rest of your life. There's no benefits to having a low omega-3 index. Based on the vast amount of research, having a low omega-3 index is only harmful. So, how much omega-3s are we talking about? The health organizations recommend consuming 250 to 500 milligs of EPA and DHA per day. A recent analysis across the world saw that Japanese consume at least 500 milligs per day, resulting in an omega-3 index above 8%. Whereas most other countries consume less than 250 milligs per day, which is why their omega-3 index is below 6%. Globally, about 85% of people are not consuming enough omega-3s. In the USA, it's around 95%. Europe, 80%, Africa and South Asia, 90%, and Japan is the only country where less than 10% of people aren't getting enough omega-3s. Just think how crazy it is. In the USA, 5% of people are getting adequate amounts of omega-3s every day. In Japan, it's 90%. If you're not eating seafood regularly, then chances are your omega-3 index is suboptimal, unless you're taking an omega-3 supplement such as some marine based omega-3s or all- based omega-3s. Another thing we need to talk about is torine. Torine is an amino acid that's also been seen to have longevity benefits. In animal studies, torine extends lifespan, and in human clinical trials, torine supplementation improves blood sugar, lipids, and blood pressure. And that's one of the dietary factors thought to contribute to the longevity of the Japanese with higher urinary torine being associated with lower heart disease mortality. The Japanese diet is high in one of the highest torine containing foods such as tuna, scallops, nori, and other sea vegetables and sea moss. In comparison, foods more often eaten in Western countries like turkey, beef, and chicken are much lower in torine, and they're also low in omega-3s. The Japanese people are probably getting two to three times more torine in addition to two to three times more omega-3s in their diet. When they're comparing omega-3s and torine, then there's a lot more evidence suggesting that omega-3s have more benefits than torine. However, both have benefits and that Japanese people eat a lot of both. As I said in the beginning, there are a lot of reasons why Japanese people live longer than others. First of all, they're less overweight and obese than Americans or Europeans. They eat better food, although their diet isn't completely unprocessed or low carb. Their Asian cuisine still comprises of high carb, refined foods as well as deep fried foods cooked in seed oils, but they seem to compensate for that with their very high omega-3 intake. Another thing is obviously good health care. Europeans also have very good health care, which is why life expectancy in European countries is still above 80s in most Western and Northern European countries, despite their omega-3 index being slightly lower at 6 to 8%. Japanese people have good healthare and a high omega-3 index, which is the best combo. Healthcare is obviously very underrated. Walking seems very simple, but it's one of the most misunderstood types of exercise. 10,000 steps a day is useless. It's a madeup thing. You don't need to walk at all. Just lift weights or do hit cardio. Check out this cool new Japanese walking technique. It beats regular walking. Let's start with what everyone has heard about 10k steps a day. We've all heard that you should walk at least 10,000 steps a day to be healthy. But the truth is that yes, the 10k steps a day recommendation came from a 1964 Japanese marketing campaign that was selling a tracking device for tracking your steps. Now, this doesn't mean that walking 10,000 steps a day is bad for your health. Quite the opposite. A 2023 meta analysis, 111,000 participants and 12 studies looked at how many steps correlates with the lowest risk of mortality and heart disease. The biggest reduction in the risk of all causality was seen when you go from walking 2,000 steps a day to walking 8,700 steps a day, which results in a 60% lower all causality risk. Going from 8,700 steps to 16,000 steps provides an an additional 5% risk reduction. This means that the bulk of the benefits of walking come from going from being a couch potato 2,000 steps a day to 8,700 steps a day, which is only 1 and 1/2 hours of walking throughout the day. You do get additional benefits by going beyond that up to 16,000, which is 5% additional benefits, but it requires doubling your step count. Walking 10k steps a day is still associated with a slightly better risk compared to 8,700 steps, but the benefits are small. 10k steps a day is just an easy huristic you can use. It's a number that you can just memorize and if you have a tracker, you can just track it. Personally, I am still aiming for around 10k steps a day. On most days, I'm probably between 9,000 and 11,000 steps, but I'm trying to go above the 8,700 steps a day because there's additional reasons to why walking more than 8,700 steps a day could be better. They saw increases in HRV with up to 20,000 steps per day. This is not a very robust clinical study, but it does show that people who walk more up to 20k steps a day have higher HRV. And because it's done only on Fitbit users, you reduce the potential for healthy user bias because everyone who has a Fitbit is already more invested and interested in a healthy lifestyle. It's not a perfect study, but it does have some insight. I personally have seen that my HRV is higher if I walk more. The results show that longer walking bouts over 15 minutes were associated with the lowest risk of mortality as well as heart disease. Even when the total daily step count remained under 8,000 steps, walking bouts shorter than 5 minutes had the highest risk. So it looks like if you do go for a walk, you should walk for over 15 minutes in a go rather than just walking for 5 minutes. So what does this interval walking look like? 3 minutes of fast walking, roughly 70% of peak aerobic capacity. three minutes of slow walking, 40% of peak aerobic capacity and repeated for five times five times per week. Basically, walking fast for three minutes and walking regularly for 3 minutes. The caveat is that this interval walking is studied in elderly people. These people can run. === FILE: The Surprising Link Between Iron Levels and Longevity [7RpMYKTDaPg].en.txt ===

Iron is an essential mineral that's needed for the production of hemoglobin in red blood cells which carries oxygen around the body. However, high iron levels are seen to be associated with increased risk of mortality and reduced lifespan. So why is something that's essential bad for your longevity? It comes down to the bifphasic response curve where not enough of something is harmful. Too much is harmful and just enough is good for you. Water, oxygen, food, sleep, they all follow that curve. There's actually a very interesting relationship between iron levels and longevity that I'm going to discuss in this video. I'm going to talk about how much iron is optimal and how to keep your iron levels normal for longevity. Let's start with the relationship between iron status and mortality. High iron status is associated with a higher risk of mortality in multiple different populations. Genetically high iron status has also been seen to be associated with a shorter lifespan. Based on this 2021 Mandelian randomization study, every standard deviation increase in iron status was seen to shorten lifespan by 0.7 years and higher iron levels reduce the odds of reaching the top 10% of lifespan. Basically, high iron status curbs the likelihood of reaching extreme longevity. Another 2020 mandelian randomization study on over 1 million people found that genetically high iron levels shortened lifespan. So there's evidence from the observational data, genetic studies as well as animal studies to suggest that iron in excess is bad for maximum longevity. The reason high iron levels are seen to shorten lifespan is because high iron increases the risk of heart disease. First and foremost, iron is a mineral that in excess can easily get oxidized, which is why high amounts of iron increases the likelihood of endothelial dysfunction and plaque accumulation in the arteries. This is also one of the reasons it's thought that men get more heart disease and live shorter than women. Women up until menopause menrate regularly, so they're losing excess iron every month. At the same time, iron restriction has been seen to extend lifespan in animal models by lowering oxidative stress and increasing autophagy, the process of removing cell debris. There's no evidence that restricting iron in humans would extend longevity, but iron gulation in patients with iron overload increases their survival. What it does confirm is that very high iron levels can be harmful for you and it can increase the risk of heart disease and liver disease specifically because that's where iron accumulates the most. One of the signs of iron accumulation are liver spots on your skin and face. These dark spots, these are actually lipopuskin which is an age related pigment that causes oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. That's why lipopuskin fits into the hallmarks of aging. Lipophuskin is basically cellular junk and high iron levels increase lipophuskin accumulation through oxidative stress. Iron is still an essential nutrient that you need for tissue oxygenation. Low iron status and iron deficiency anemia are also associated with increased risk of mortality, especially in people with cardiovascular complications. People who are most likely to die from iron deficiency are old people because their iron deficiency is usually because of overall malnutrition and not eating enough food. Young women can also be deficient in iron, especially if they're menstruating regularly and they don't get enough iron from their food. But this doesn't appear to increase the risk of mortality that much because they're otherwise healthy and otherwise young. So if you were to play devil's advocate, then you could even say that it's not necessarily the iron deficiency that is associated with increased mortality. It's the malnutrition that causes iron deficiency. And malnutrition also walks handinhand with other nutrient deficiencies as well as frailty and sarcopenia. Otherwise, you would see a lot of young women dropping dead from iron deficiency, which clearly doesn't happen. This is what a 2024 study actually found. They looked at over 5,000 patients around the age of 75 and saw that only in those with anemia was iron deficiency associated with increased mortality. In non-anmic individuals, low iron wasn't seen to increase mortality risk. So, what's the difference between anemia and iron deficiency? Iron deficiency refers to low blood iron status due to either not getting enough dietary iron or having some other malabsorption condition that results in lower iron absorption. It could also be because of menstruation or excessive bleeding for other reasons. Anemia is a condition of inadequate hemoglobin the protein that carries oxygen around the body. In adult men, hemoglobin less than 13 g per deciliter and in women less than 12 g per deciliter is defined as anemia. Anemia can be because of iron deficiency, which is when it's called iron deficiency anemia. But it can also be because of other reasons such as autoimmunity or bone marrow disorders. So how much iron are we talking about? Like with other biomarkers, there's a sweet spot. Not too much, not too little, just enough. The normal reference range for iron is 50 to 150 micrograms per deciliter for males and 35 to 145 micrograms per deciliter for females. Iron in that range would reduce the risk of iron becoming harmful. However, it's often seen that iron slightly on the lower end, not deficient, but around 60 to 90 micrograms per deciliter is associated with the lowest mortality risk. Iron below 45 and above 145 micrograms per deciliter is associated with increased risk of mortality. For hemoglobin, the normal range is 13.5 to 17.5 for men and 12 to 15.5 g per deciliter for women. below 13 and 12 grams per deciliter is anemia and associated with increased mortality. A more optimal hemoglobin range is 14 to 16 grams per deciliter. There are also other biomarkers that relate to iron status such as transfer and saturation feritin and total iron binding capacity TIBC, but I'm not going into the details in this video. The main thing is that too much iron is bad, not enough iron is bad, and you want to be in the sweet spot. It's got 24 chapters on all aspects of longevity, and it's based on over 8,000 scientific references. What I want to do in the rest of this video is talk about how can you then achieve more optimal iron status. Iron can be low because of either not eating enough iron from food or having some malabsorption condition that reduces iron absorption. You can get iron from meat in the most bioavailable form as he iron with an absorption rate of 15 to 35%. But you could also get iron from leafy greens and other plants, but this iron is non-heem with an absorption rate of 1 to 15%. So you would need a lot more of the iron from plants, which is why plant-based diets can increase the risk of iron deficiency. That can be a good or bad thing depending on what your blood iron actually is. Vitamin C enhances iron absorption, which can also be a good or bad thing depending on your iron status. If you're deficient in iron or you're eating a plant-based diet, then vitamin C from fruits and vegetables or supplements can increase iron absorption. Eating meat with vitamin C, like oranges or orange juice could result in too much iron absorption, but that depends on your blood iron status. Coffee and teas reduce iron absorption because they contain different compounds that bind to iron. That can be a good or bad thing depending on your iron status. If you are iron deficient, then minimize the consumption of coffee and teas around meals to prevent iron gilation. If you are high in iron, then drinking coffee with your meat, for example, could be good to lower iron absorption. Hemoglobin status is influenced by other minerals as well, not just iron. Mostly, it's copper because kerolopplasmine, which is a major copper carrying protein in the blood, increases iron absorption and hemoglobin production. Anemia could in fact be because of copper deficiency instead of iron because iron is extremely easy to get from food. You can get copper from foods like liver, oysters, clams, dark chocolate, and beans. So sometimes trying to get more iron isn't going to fix low hemoglobin. Sometimes you need more copper. In fact, it's more likely you need more copper rather than more iron. Overall, the main message of this video is that too much of anything can be bad, even essential minerals. But if you're not getting enough of something that can also be equally as harmful. A lot of biomarkers, nutrients, and activities follow this similar bifphasic response curve. Not too much, not too little, just enough. This bifphasic response curve is a ubiquitous phenomenon in biology. === FILE: The Surprising Link Between Short Sleep and Longevity [OI1YyKQtPzM].en.txt ===

I recently came across a surprising statistic that Japanese people sleep on average 352 minutes or 5.8 hours a night. Yet, there are people with the highest life expectancy of 85.27 years. South Koreans also sleep on average 6 hours a night with a life expectancy of 84.5 years. That's 5 years longer than people in other Western countries. I'm not saying that this is the reason why Japanese and Koreans live so long or that everyone literally sleeps 6 hours there. But it's just surprising given the fact how much people say that you need to sleep 8 hours every night to be healthy. So I decided to dig up the research again and look at how much sleep do you actually need and how many hours of sleep is associated with the lowest mortality and the greatest longevity. The general recommendation for sleep is 7 to 8 hours for adults. However, many of the observational studies find that the lowest mortality risk is actually seen at 7 hours per night. A 2016 meta analysis of 35 studies saw that 7 hours per night was associated with the lowest mortality risk. And sleeping less than 6 hours or more than 8 hours was associated with increased risk. Interestingly, sleeping over 8 hours is associated with a much higher risk than sleeping less than 6 hours. That's because people who sleep over 8 hours usually have some sort of a disease or sickness like cancer or they're near their deathbed. Long sleep is associated with increased risk of diabetes, heart disease, and stroke. This is the reason why sleeping 7 hours appears to be associated with the lowest mortality and why Japanese people can get away with sleeping only 6 hours per night. === FILE: The Surprising Science Between Height and Longevity [rwwXz4ygS7g].en.txt ===

There's a very interesting relationship between height, growth hormone, and longevity that I wanted to talk about. Let's start with one of the biggest humans in history. Andre the giant was 7'4 in or 224 cm tall who weighed 520 lb or 236 kilos. He was a giant quite literally because of suffering from a genetic condition called gigantism that made him produce excessive amounts of growth hormone. This made him grow and he had enormous hands and feet which is called acromegaly. Growth hormone plays an important role in growth and development during puberty and childhood. Growth hormone stimulates the production of IGF-1 that then mediates bone growth, muscle mass, and makes you grow. How much growth hormone and IGF-1 you're exposed to during development determines your overall height. How you respond to this surge is influenced by genetics and childhood nutrition. However, how much growth hormone and IG-1 you're exposed to during developmental years has also been seen to determine the organism's lifespan and producing less growth hormone results in longer life in mice. In humans, acromegali is associated with a higher risk of cancer, heart disease, and overall mortality. People with acromegaly have a twofold higher mortality risk compared to the general population. Andre didn't live for very long. He died at the age of 46 to congestive heart failure due to his enlarged heart from acromegaly called cardomegalgaly. There's also the opposite condition of insufficient growth hormone and nitro production during developmental years which is called lon syndrome. People with luron syndrome live average lifespans 70 to 80 years but they have a much lower risk of cancer and diabetes than the general population because of low IGF-1 levels. So you have this very interesting situation where people with excessive growth hormone production live shorter and they get more chronic diseases especially cancer and heart failure. Whereas people with less growth hormone production or insufficient growth hormone production live longer and they have less chronic diseases especially cancer. When it comes to animals than larger animals like whales and humans typically live longer than shorter animals like mice and dogs. However, smaller individuals within species live longer than larger individuals of that species. For example, smaller dogs live twice as long as large dogs. While a great Dne's life expectancy is 6 to 8 years, a Chihuahua is 10 to 18 years. Larger dogs are also more prone to most of the chronic diseases, especially cancer and osteoporosis. But what about humans? Is there any evidence that being shorter and smaller in body weight is beneficial for longevity in humans? In the past, height was a good indicator of socioeconomic status and better living conditions, resulting in longer life. This Spanish study saw that in the years 1835 to 1869, men over 170 cm or 5'7 in lived 7.6 years longer than men shorter than 160 cm or 5'3 in because height was determined by socioeconomic status and living conditions. The difference in life expectancy disappeared in those born between 1900 to 1939, mostly because living standards and medical care improved for everyone. This 2002 study on baseball players saw that shorter individuals lived longer, even though everyone's life expectancy had increased since the beginning of the 20th century. What enhances fitness early in life may have harmful effects on lifespan later in life and vice versa. Growth hormone and nigan support growth and proper development early in life. But later in life, they increase the risk of cancer and mortality. The reason antagonistic pleotropy exists is because evolution doesn't care how long you live. It doesn't care about your maximum lifespan. Evolution only cares about short-term reproductive success so you can carry on your genes to the next generation. That's why what favors short-term survival in the reproductive years and developmental years might not necessarily be optimal for maximum lifespan. There is evidence for antagonistic pleotropy in humans as well. This study on 276,000 UK individuals saw that individuals with higher polygenetic scores for reproduction have lower survivorships to age 76. Basically, people with higher genetic reproductive traits are less likely to survive until the age of 76. Those with a low score are the most likely to live past 76, at least in this cohort of people. Weighted vests have become insanely popular. I've got a 5 kilo vest here, a 30 kilo vest here, and I've been using them for over a year in my training, on my hikes, and especially for building stronger pull-ups. But here's the thing. A weighted vest isn't just a fitness fat. There's actually fascinating research showing how simply wearing a weighted vest in your daily life can improve strength, metabolism, and long-term health. In this video, I'll break down the science, share my own experience, and help you decide whether or not adding a weighted vest is worthwhile for you. The first and most obvious benefit of weighted vests is that they just help you to burn more calories because you have to carry them around. A 2024 study took 20 healthy, physically active military-aged adults and made them walk for 6 to 21 minutes with four different weighted vests. What they found was that the higher the weight they carried, the more calories they burned. Having a 22% of body weight vest increased energy expenditure by 12.4%. Having a 44% bodyweight vest increased energy expenditure by 25.7%. And having a 66% body weight vest increased energy burn by 41.2%. For me who weighs 80 kg, 66% body weight would be 52 kg, which is quite a lot. But a 41% higher calorie burn is also insane. My current weighted vest is 30 kg max, and I can comfortably walk and even run in it, but 52 kg would be quite more strenuous. The researchers also saw that a weighted backpack is even more powerful than a weighted vest for some reason. For every 10% body weight added, rock sacking increased energy burn by 19.6% compared to the 13.8% of a weighted vest. It's probably because walking with a weighted backpack is harder and you have to exert more energy for balance. So, how many calories are we talking about? For the most energy expenditure, the subjects had to walk 1.5 to 2 m/s, which is the average walking speed. If you walked 2 meters per second for one hour without a weight, you would burn around 410 calories. With a 22% body weight vest, you would burn 520 calories. With a 44% bodyweight vest, you would burn 660 calories. And with a 66% body weight vest, you would burn 820 calories. That's twice as much as you would burn without a vest, which is quite insane. From my own personal experience, I can say that walking with a 30 kg weighted vest is quite simple. It's not extremely difficult that I couldn't do it. I'm of course quite fit and I have good cardiorespiratory fitness and good muscle strength. So, it's not expected to be difficult for me. My heart rate does increase to the low 100s, which is something like zone one heart rate for me. So, it's not even considered strenuous exercise. So, it feels like you're walking up a hill or hiking. Another perk of walking with a veed vest or rock sacking is that it's less strenuous on your joints. If you have knee pain or something like that and you can't run, then you can easily replace it with a weighted vest and get decent cardio. So, for weight loss, walking with a weighted vest is better than regular walking. However, using a weighted vest during weight loss has been seen to prevent weight regain after you stop dieting. This 2025 pilot study on older adults aged 70 who were obese and with osteoarthritis found that not only did those who wore a weighted vest during dieting lost more weight by the 6-month mark, minus 11.2 2 kg versus - 10.3 kg. But they also gained back only 50% of the weight they lost after 2 years. Whereas those who just dieted gained all of their weight back and even gained 900 g. The interesting thing here is that after 6 months of wearing the weighted vest, the resting metabolic rate decreased by only 16 calories, whereas the group without the weighted vest saw a 237 calorie drop in the resting metabolic rate. That's a 200 calorie difference, which over the long term will have a huge effect on their body composition and health. The reason for this is probably because when you lose weight, your resting metabolic rate will inevitably decrease because you lose weight. If you weigh less, your body requires less energy to survive and thus your metabolic rate lowers. However, if you're wearing a weighted vest, this 30 kg beast, you have to carry this goddamn thing around and therefore you exert more energy to carry it. You're basically tricking your body into thinking you weigh more than you really do. Because your body only recognizes the force it has to exert every day, not how much you actually weigh, your resting metabolic rate stays elevated. Okay, so what's the protocol? The participants wore a weighted vest based on how much weight they had lost to keep their weight the same from the beginning. They increase the weight every week up to a maximum of 15% of their baseline weight. For an 80 kg person, that's only 12 kg, which isn't a lot. The catch is that they were told to wear the west on average 6 to8 hours per day, which sounds like a lot, but the average weight the participants actually wore was 6 kg or 7.3% of their baseline body weight, and they did it on average for 2 to 3 hours a day. So, in my opinion, this is another win for the weighted vest. Not only do you lose more weight by wearing the weighted vest, even as little as 5 to 6 kg, but you also prevent your resting metabolic rate from decreasing during the weight loss. Because wearing a weighted vest overloads your joints, it might also increase your bone density. And because you lose bone density during weight loss because you have to carry less mass around, wearing a weighted vest might also prevent the loss of bone density. In this 2025 randomized control trial, they saw that 12 months of weight loss with a weighted vest of up to 10% body weight didn't prevent the bone loss in older adults. But the weighted vest group did maintain a little bit more bone mass, although it wasn't statistically significant. Previous studies on post-menopausal women have found that weighted vests can reduce bone loss. So, there might be some minor effects. Based on the current evidence, wearing a weighted vest isn't going to prevent bone loss, but it might slow it down. And some bone loss is to be expected when you're losing weight. You can just minimize it with a weighted vest. Like I said, I've been using a weighted vest in my training for many years. In most cases, I use it for doing weighted pull-ups and weighted dips. And it's amazing for getting stronger at calisthenics. I don't wear a weighted vest every day when I'm walking or something like that because I'm not trying to lose weight, but I do like to wear my weighted vest for some walks and hikes as just zone one cardio. Overall, I definitely like my weighted vest. I'm going to keep using it in my training and in my walking. And I do think a lot of people would benefit from wearing a weighted vest. For daily use, something like 10 to 15% of your body weight will make it a lot easier to lose weight and increase your conditioning without doing specifically cardio. Glucosamine is often thought to be like a gimmick supplement. It's what all people take for their joints and bone health. But after digging into the research, I noticed something unexpected. Glucosamine and related compounds like MSM and chondroitin may actually be better for skin anti-aging than for joints. Once you understand some of the biology, it makes perfect sense. So, in this video, I'm going to share with you why these joint supplements might also belong in the skin anti-aging category. So, glucosamine is one of those supplements everyone's grandma is taking similar to omega-3s. It's a bit controversial, but there are clinical trials showing that glucosamine supplementation improves pain and joint function to a moderate to large degree in osteoarthritis patients. Glucosamine is needed for the synthesis of cartilage glycosaminoglycans gags which function as lubricants or shock absorbers for the joints. In arthritis, cartilage gags have decreased sulfate content. That's why glucosamine sulfate is the best form of glucosamine to take for joint health. It's the sulfur element. But the sulfur is also the reason why glucosamine has also been seen to have skin benefits. Sulfur supports the production of glutathione, which is a powerful antioxidant in the body. Glutathione is what's often used in skin care for whitening the skin and reducing hyperpigmentation. But the antioxidant effects of glutathione would also counteract skin wrinkles by lowering oxidative stress. In a 2017 clinical trial, women taking 250 milligs of glucosamine sulfate a day for 8 weeks saw improved wrinkles and higher collagen synthesis. In the cell culture part of the study, glucosamine sulfate was seen to increase GA levels in the epidermis and collagen synthesis which provides a mechanistic explanation for the results. Glucosamine specifically inhibits matrix metalloproinases MMPs which are one of the primary things that degrade skin collagen. To be honest, there's not that many randomized control trials on glucosamine supplementation and skin and aging, but there are a lot more studies on the other sulfur compounds that I'm going to talk about. Methyl sulfenylmethane MSM is a sulfur molecule with anti-inflammatory properties, which is why it's been shown to improve osteoarthritis pain and joint health. There are several randomized control trials showing that MSM improves joint function, pain, and stiffness. The typical dose is 1.5 to six grams per day divided into two to three doses. Combining MSM with glucosamine appears to be superior to either alone. So does MSM also have skin benefits? Then in a 2022 pilot study, MSM supplementation at a dose of 1 to 3 g per day for 16 weeks reduced wrinkles, decreased skin roughness, improved elasticity, firmness, and hydration. A 2015 randomized control trial of three grams of MSM also shows similar benefits. We have talked about the benefits of collagen on skin anti-aging on this channel. But adding 1.5 g of MSM to 5 or 10 g of collagen peptides has been shown to improve the skin dermis density, skin texture, and reduce wrinkles in a 2023 clinical trial. MSM alone was more effective in increasing skin thickness and roughness than 10 g of hydrayed fish collagen. The best results across all parameters were seen with 10 grams of hydrayzeed collagen peptides with 1.5 grams of MSM. Thanks to its antioxidant and glutathione boosting benefits, MSM might also protect the skin against sun damage. In a 2022 study, mice were exposed to UVB radiation for 6 weeks, and the ones getting MSM showed fewer wrinkles and photoagging compared to nothing. MSM mice also showed less collagen confirmation loss and more androgenesis and elastin precursors than saline or retinoic acid. So MSM has a lot more evidence for skin benefits compared to glucosamine. But the actions are very similar. These sulfur compounds protect the skin against damage whether that damage come from the sun or other sources like aging. And these sulfur compounds also stimulate the production of collagen and elastin. Let's talk about the third sulfur compound chondroitin. Chondroitin sulfate is a structural component of cartilage and it's a sulfated glycosaminoglycin. Chondroitin sulfate improves the ability of the joints to resist compression. A 2015 cockrine review of 43 randomized control trials saw that chondroitin provides small to moderate effects in improving pain and function in osteoarthritis as well as reduce joint space width. When it comes to skin anti-aging, there are no human studies on chondroitin yet. However, in cell studies, chondroitin sulfate stimulates the expression of type 1 procolagen and the proliferation of keratinosytes and fiberlasts which promote wound healing and skin regeneration. As you can see, there's quite compelling evidence from mechanistic studies as well as some human clinical trials that these sulfur compounds glucosamine, MSM, and chondroitin have some benefits on skin anti-aging. We definitely would need more random control trials on this topic. And I'm not saying that everyone should go out there and start taking glucosamine for skin health. It's not very likely that glucosamine or MSM is more effective for skin health compared to something like collagen peptides or asexandin. They might improve or enhance the results that you're getting, but they're not going to be better than retinol or sunscreen or something else like that. However, these skin effects are more like bonus benefits. The way I think about it, these sulfur compounds are generally anti-inflammatory, which is one of the main reasons you would want to take them. They improved skin health. They reduce wrinkles are just a bonus. Supplementing glucosamine is associated with a 39% lower risk of all cause mortality and lower heart disease events and cancer. Obviously, these are observational studies, but usually if people take glucosamine, they do it because they have some joint pain or some joint issues. So, elderly people with joint pain. So, this isn't your classical healthy user bias because most people who take glucosamine have joint pain. No one really takes glucosamine for preventive health or health optimization. The mechanistic effects of glucosamine also suggest it has direct anti-inflammatory effects. Supplementing with glucosamine hydrochloride and chondroitin sulfate can lower inflammation as measured by CRP by 23% as seen in a 2015 clinical trial. === FILE: The Workout That Makes Your Heart 20 Years Younger [mt5AQnZeSCo].en.txt ===

What if I told you your heart has an age and you can make it younger? An aging heart becomes stiffer, pumps less efficiently, and loses its ability to respond to stress. Your max heart rate drops, stroke volume decreases, and the blood vessels stiffen. But here's the exciting part. Scientists have discovered a workout that can make your heart up to 20 years younger. It sounds too good to be true, but it's true. A 2018 randomized control trial took 60 healthy, sedentary, middle-aged people in their 50s, and they were randomly assigned to either two years of structured exercise training or a control group that was getting non-cardiovascular exercise such as yoga, stretching, balance, and flexibility. Those who exercised saw significant improvements in their V2 max, their fitness, and overall heart functioning. Their left ventricular chamber stiffness reduced by about 29% and myioardial stiffness decreased by about 20% from baseline whereas the control group saw no reduction and theirs even increased slightly. The reduction in left ventricular chamber stiffness corresponds to a 20-year reversal in the structure of the heart. They reverted back to the stiffness of a 35year-old which was 20 years younger than their chronological age of mid-50s. While it's just one marker, it's quite impressive. And if I was in my 50s, I would definitely want to get a heart of a 35year-old. So what was their workout? For the first one to two months, they just acclimated to working out and they did three times 30 minutes steadystate cardio per week at 60 to 75% of their max heart rate. During months 3 to 10, they introduced [clears throat] highintensity interval training, specifically the 4x4 Norwegian protocol. four times four minutes at 90 to 95% max heart rate, three minutes of active recovery between the intervals, and one to two sessions per week. By month six, their weekly workout plan looked like this. Two times interval sessions, the 4x4 hit, one time long base sessions over 60 minutes at the lower intensity, one moderate base session of 30 minutes, two strength training sessions targeting core and whole body, and one recovery/walking day. Months 11 to 24, they maintained their training load and reduced HIT to one session per week. However, they continued aerobic training and resistance training. That's a pretty solid workout, and I think that everyone can do it. Those who exercised saw an 18% increase in their V2 max from 29 ml per kilogram per minute to 34.4. Their aerobic capacity and overall fitness improved significantly. Whereas the control group who did no cardiovascular exercise saw slight age related decline in their V2 max from 29.5 to 28.7 and their fitness decreased. An increase in V2 max by 18% isn't that significant especially after 2 years of training and especially given the fact that their baseline where they started from was already quite low but they definitely improved their fitness. It might be that because they were already in their 50s, their body just couldn't increase their V2 max any further because their V2 max plateaued already in the middle of the study. However, they also just plan to maintain their fitness after the first year. And they did decrease the frequency of high-intensity interval training. What it means is that the longer you wait to increase your V2X, the harder it becomes and the less gains you can expect. If you start doing V2AX training in your 60s, 70s or 80s, then you'll get far fewer results than someone who started doing it in their 30s. Their left ventricular end diastolic volume index which reflects the functioning of the left ventricular of the heart increased by 7.1 ml per square meter whereas the control group saw a decrease of 1.0. So the exercise group saw much better heart functioning. The resting heart rate also dropped by 4 to six beats per minute. They saw other improvements in their heart functioning as well. Effective arterial elastins reduced from 2.37 to 2.16 which means their heart had to work less hard. Arterial compliance increased from 1.07 to 1.29 which reflects the elasticity of the arteries. Stroke volume improved and plasma volume and hemoglobin also improved. So overall their heart functioning improved significantly whereas the control group who did just stretching and just mobility exercises experienced aging of the heart. Their heart health got worse. So what's the magic source here? The key component is near maximum exercise such as the 4x4 Norwegian protocol. It doesn't necessarily have to be that specific protocol, but the key component is taking your heart rate close to its maximum. That's the reason the people who did stretching and mobility didn't experience any benefits. They never raise their heart rate to close to its maximum. It means that to reverse your cardiac age, you need to be doing some form of high-intensity interval training. The Norwegian protocol utilizes 4 minutes at your absolute near peak heart rate, which depends on your age. A standard method to calculate your max heart rate is to subtract your age from 220. I'm 31, so my max heart rate based on my age would be 189. For me, the 90 to 95% of max heart rate is 170 to 179 beats per minute. The older you are, the lower your estimated max heart rate is going to be because of aging. But if you're fitter, then your max heart rate can also be higher than expected for your chronological age. It's essentially use it or lose it. If you don't take your heart rate close to its maximum every once in a while, then your max heart rate is just going to decrease and it means that your heart functioning is getting worse. The reason this HIT protocol reversed cardiac structure is because the hemodynamic load and mechanical stress from a hard beating heart stretches the left ventricular walls. It makes the heart work more efficiently and restructures it making the heart less stiff. The authors of the study saw that the heart maintains its ability to reverse the stiffness up until the age of 65. After the age of 65, the collagen cross-linking becomes more permanent and it becomes harder to reverse the cardiac stiffness. So, the younger you start, the better it is. Zone 2 probably had less of a role in restructuring the heart and lowering cardiac age, but it's still important for building a solid aerobic base. So, you should do both forms of training. === FILE: This Longevity Drug Might Be Destroying Your Exercise Results [GzZxEOuPII0].en.txt ===

Metformin is one of the most popular longevity drugs on the planet. Many people take it not just for diabetes, but hoping that it'll make them live longer. But here's the twist you probably haven't heard about. Several studies now suggest that metformin may actually cancel out some of the benefits from exercise, the very thing that is supposed to make you live longer. Just recently, there was a 16week double blind placebo control trial on people with metabolic syndrome. And they found that those who exercised while taking metformin saw blunted benefits from the exercise. There were four groups in total. Low inensity exercise plus placebo, low inensity exercise plus metformin, high-intensity exercise plus placebo, and high-intensity exercise plus metformin. V2x improved only in the placebo groups, not in the metformin groups. Body fat decreased in both the highintensity groups regardless of metformin, but not in the low inensity group. Placebo groups who exercised saw improved flow media dilation and microvascular blood flow both of which are indicators of vascular function and incidentivity. Metformin groups however saw no significant increase in these markers. Metformin also blunted the reductions in fasting glucose ET1 and TNF alpha compared to placebo exercise. That's quite shocking if you think about it. Just because the individuals were taking metformin, they saw less benefits from exercise and some of the benefits they avoided altogether. What it means is that arguably metformin is a net negative for otherwise healthy people who don't need it for diabetes. I'm going to discuss the potential benefits of metformin as a longevity compound later in this video. But this is not the first study showing that metformin reduces the benefits from exercise. Another 2020 randomized control trial on adults over 65 saw that taking metformin while resistance training blunted muscle hypertrophy and gene expression related to muscle growth. And an even earlier trial saw the same results. Older adults taking metformin built less muscle and strength compared to the placebo group. So if someone is doing resistance training and they're taking metformin, they appear to see less benefits on muscle growth and they also see less insulin sensitivity caused by the exercise. However, there are several studies showing that metformin reduces muscle loss during this use, like bed rest or hospitalization. This is extremely interesting. If you take Metformin while lifting weights, you build less muscle. But if you take Metformin when you're not lifting weights when you're hospitalized and you have immobilization, then Metformin reduces the muscle loss that happens because of disuse. But why is this so? Well, it's probably because metformin is a potent mTor inhibitor. mTor is the main growth switch in the body that gets activated during exercise. MTTOR is absolutely critical to muscle growth as it increases protein synthesis, the growth of new muscle tissue. If you inhibit mTor after exercise, you won't build muscle. That's why you're not going to build muscle by fasting or eating a low calorie diet. However, during bed rest and disuse, metformin prevents muscle loss by activating the pathway of muscle preservation. And it also helps to eliminate scinesscent cells that cause inflammation. By lowering inflammation, muscle loss signaling decreases. But because metformin interferes with the recovery pathways such as mTor, you see this dual effect. Anti-anabolic effects from metformin when you're lifting weights. But anti catabolic effects if you're not lifting weights. When it comes to V2 max, then similar effects are true. Besides the study I showed earlier, several studies show that metformin reduces exercise capacity and peak aerobic capacity during exercise. Metformin impairs mitochondrial function especially at complex one of the electron transport chain which reduces ATP production efficiency and limits v2ax during intense exercise. So if someone is trying to build muscle or increase their v2 max then they should definitely avoid metformin. Both VOTMAX and muscle strength are components of longevity and people with higher VOMX and muscle strength live longer. So if you're taking Metformin while trying to increase your VOMAX and muscle strength, then you're jeopardizing some of your results. I understand if someone is taking metformin for the sake of diabetes, there is evidence that Metformin reduces the risk of mortality in diabetics. But based on the evidence that I shared with you right now, it's arguable whether metformin will be a longevity compound for otherwise healthy people who are already exercising. In type 2 diabetics, metformin has been clearly and consistently been shown to reduce mortality, cancer, and heart disease. Where longevity enthusiasts got excited was when a 2014 study showed that metforming users with diabetes had a lower mortality risk than non-diabetics who weren't taking metformin. Now, if you think about it for a second, then it just sounds very bizarre. Diabetics who had diabetes while they were taking metformin lived longer than the otherwise healthy people who weren't taking metformin. This is quite crazy if you think about it. Diabetes is a disease that shortens your life expectancy by about 5 to 10 years. And based on the findings of this study, metformin would be so powerful that it makes up for this 5 to 10 years shorter life expectancy and even adds on top of that it increases the life expectancy compared to regular healthy people. Fortunately, a 2022 study reanalyzed the initial 2014 study and discovered that diabetics taking metformin didn't in fact live longer than non-diabetics not taking Metformin. The reason for the discrepancy was that the initial study has some confounding variables and selection bias that were fixed in the reanalysis. The interventions testing program studies on metformin have also shown that it doesn't really extend lifespan in mice. Metformin only extends lifespan if combined with rapamy. Metformin doesn't extend lifespan in heterogeneous mice, which means mice that are genetically diverse. It only extends lifespan in certain mice with certain genes. With all of that being said, it's hard to say that Metformin would be a longevity compound, especially for otherwise healthy people who don't have diabetes. First of all, the evidence from observational studies is very limited. And second of all, if you look at the components of longevity, such as Vtoax and muscle strength, then metformin appears to be a negative for people who are otherwise healthy. Do I think metformin has some use case in non-diabetics? Yes, there are some situations where taking metformin can be useful. For example, the situations where you're not exercising and you're not lifting weights. If you are immobilized or you go for a longer period of time without exercising then yes metformin can be a net positive. Coincidentally all the longevity gurus or scientists that promote metformin are also the ones who don't exercise. So for these individuals maybe metformin is a positive. But if you are someone who exercises regularly and you are trying to improve your body composition your max and your muscle strength and muscle mass then metformin based on these studies is generally a net negative. I ranked Metformin and 100 other supplements from worst to best based on their benefits and evidence from studies.

=== FILE: Watch This Before Trying to Lose Visceral Fat [X-WZWMH7WZs].en.txt ===

Reducing your visceral fat around the organs can be one of the most beneficial things for your long-term cardiovascular disease and diabetes risk. I have very low visceral fat, only 54 grams, which means that my metabolic health, insulin sensitivity, and organ function is excellent. I've achieved such low visceral fat by adjusting my diet and exercise based on the clinical studies out there. But in this video, I want to refute some of the misconceptions and misinformation about reducing visceral fat. What increases it and how do you reduce it? I'll cover things like carbohydrates, fructose, exercise, cardio, coffee, and fats. The first lie or misconception is that you need to be on a low carb diet to reduce visceral fat. To not only avoid eating sugar and refined carbohydrates, but also any carbohydrates, and that the only way to lose visceral fat is to be on a low carb diet. The truth is that visceral fat is more affected by total calorie intake and your body weight than the carbohydrate percentage of your diet. I eat 300 grams of carbs per day from fruit, potatoes, vegetables, some grains, and yet I have very low visceral fat. The biggest reason for that is that I'm just very lean, insulin sensitive, and I don't overeat calories. Now, I might be just like an anomaly or there might be some genetic differences, which is why we have to look at the studies done on other people. This 2019 study saw that if you ate the same amount of calories and you replaced total carbohydrates with the same amount of calories from fat, you saw an increase in visceral fat and liver fat values. Replacing 5% of total calories from carbohydrates for dietary fat was seen to increase visceral fat by 0.42 L and liver fat by 23%. The higher carb diets were associated with the lowest visceral fat and the highfat diets were associated with the highest visceral fat mass. Now, the shortcoming of this study is that it's not a randomized control trial. It's a cross-sectional analysis from a cohort in South Germany. But we do have some randomized control trials that I'll cover shortly. The most important thing that matters is total calorie intake. The higher the calorie intake, the higher the amount of visceral fat mass these people had. That's just logical. If you're eating too many calories and you're overweight, you're just going to have more visceral fat. However, the additional wrinkle of detail is that if those calories are coming more from fat and less from carbohydrates, the ratio of visceral fat mass tends to increase in not only this analysis but others as well. And keep in mind in this study, they controlled for the calorie intake. We also have a 2022 randomized control trial looking at different carbohydrate ratios for reducing visceral fat. They had three groups of carbohydrate intake. a high carb, low-fat diet with 42 to 44% carbohydrates and 36 to 38% fat comprised mostly of refined grains like bread and pasta. The second group was a whole foods high carb diet with 41 to 42% carbs and 37 to 38% fat comprised of minimally processed carbs like tubers, fruits, whole grains, etc. And a third low carb high-fat diet with 11 to 15% carbs and 66 to 70% fat. All the groups ate the same amount of calories, 2,000 calories per day for women and 2500 calories per day for men. What they found was that in 6 months, the refined high carb diet lost 14% visceral fat in 6 months and 12% in 12 months. The whole foods high carb diet lost 18% visceral fat in 6 months and 17% in 12 months. And the low carb highfat diet lost 17% visceral fat in 6 months and 13% in 12 months. Overall, there wasn't much difference in the visceral fat loss, although the whole food high carb diet trended towards the greatest loss. Carbohydrate quality does appear to matter a little bit. In this 2022 analysis of the Predimett Plus randomized control trial, they found that among overweight and obese adults with metabolic syndrome, improving carbohydrate quality was associated with favorable changes in visceral fat and overall fat deposition. The increased carbohydrate quality was reflected in eating more dietary fiber and whole grains as well as eating less refined grains and refined carbohydrates. My point here isn't that you can't lose visceral fat on a low carb or a highfat diet. You clearly can as long as you're in a calorie deficit. What I am doing is pointing out the idea that you can't lose visceral fat on a high carb diet, which clearly isn't the case, as shown by many randomized control trials. Based on these studies, a high carb diet actually results in greater visceral fat loss than a low carb diet, especially if the high carb diet is mostly based on whole food carbohydrates. The second point that is often brought up is that you shouldn't do any cardio if you want to lose visceral fat. You should just do weightlifting and walking because cardio increases cortisol. It's going to keep you stressed out and it's going to prevent you from losing any fat, not to mention visceral fat. Well, is it true? The truth is actually the complete opposite. A 2024 meta analysis of 84 randomized control trials saw that all types of exercises were able to reduce visceral fat. However, some were better than others. Here's what they discovered about which exercise decreased visceral fat the most. Highintensity interval training resulted in about 30 to 35% reduction in visceral fat. Aerobic exercise resulted also in 30 to 35% reduction. Resistance training alone resulted in 25 to 30% reduction. Resistance training plus aerobic exercise resulted in 28 to 32% reduction and minimal aerobic training such as hiking and walking resulted in 22 to 27% reduction. So cardio whether that be high-intensity interval training or aerobic exercise like zone 2 cardio decreases visceral fat significantly more than resistance training alone. Again, any type of exercise, both exercise, both weights and cardio can and will decrease visceral fat. It's just that the idea that you can't lose visceral fat when doing cardio or that cardio is worse for visceral fat than resistance training is just not true. It's the complete opposite. Based on the clinical trials, aerobic exercise is significantly more effective in reducing visceral fat than resistance training. And if you combine resistance training with aerobic exercise, you lose more visceral fat than with resistance training alone. In a 2013 meta analysis, they saw that you need a certain threshold of aerobic intensity to see a significant reduction in visceral fat, which was above 60 and 70% of max heart rate. This is the zone 2 range for heart rate, where you're not out of breath or gasping for air completely, but you're still able to breathe through the nose during exercise. The next boogeyman is fructose. And I'm not only talking about industrial fructose or high fructose corn syrup, but also natural whole fruit. I agree that you know industrial fructose from sodas and sugar cemented beverages as well as high fructose corn syrup is not good for your liver health is not good for your visceral fat. I think most people can agree with that. High fructose corn syrup and fructose consumption is seen to be associated with visceral fat. But that's not the case with fruit from whole foods. A 2024 randomized control trial on obese patients with type 2 diabetes saw that a diet intervention that included increased fruit consumption resulted in significant visceral fat loss of about 200 grams and a 2.7% decrease in liver fat. These people were in a 600 calorie deficit, which you know makes it obvious why they lost the visceral fat, but it highlights that eating fruit and increasing your fruit consumption isn't going to stop you from losing visceral fat if you're in a calorie deficit. But it doesn't seem that you need to lose weight to lose visceral fat when eating fruit. In this 2023 randomiz control trial, they found that increasing daily fruit and vegetable intake to over eight servings per day improved metabolic health and visceral fat markers even without weight loss. Now, they didn't lose visceral fat per se because they weren't in an energy deficit by design, but their inflammatory profile improved, which would indicate a healthier fat profile. In observational studies, fruit intake is inversely associated with visceral fat, meaning that higher fruit intake is seen to be associated with lower visceral fat with a maximum reduction seen at 1.5 to 2.5 servings of fruit per day. Beyond three servings, the visceral fat reduction plateaus. I'm not bringing this up to say that everyone needs to eat fruit to lose visceral fat. That's clearly not the case. Many people can lose visceral fat without eating fruit. But the idea that eating fruit is somehow uniquely damaging to your visceral fat or that you can't lose any visceral fat when eating fruit is simply not the case. The real world data suggests that people who eat moderate amounts of fruit have the least amount of visceral fat and replacing other calories with fruit tends to help with visceral fat reduction, not hinder it. The final misconception is that drinking coffee will increase visceral fat or prevent you from losing it. Again, related to cortisol. If that were the case, then why is coffee consumption associated with less visceral fat? Drinking over five cups of coffee per day has been seen to be associated with the lowest odds of visceral fat in this 2025 cross-sectional study. And this study was done in Japan, which isn't a coffee drinking culture and is not part of what's considered a healthy lifestyle in Japan. We also have some randomized control trials showing that drinking lightly roasted polyphenol rich coffee for four weeks led to a statistically significant reduction in visceral fat by up to 130 g compared to placebo. The reason coffee appears to have these benefits on visceral fat and liver fat is because of its polyphenol content. So coffee doesn't increase visceral fat, it actually decreases it. Like I said, I've managed to take my visceral fat levels to very low, only 54 g. That's the lowest I've seen anyone have. I'm not making any health claims that you need to be that low, but I have managed to decrease my visceral fat to very low levels by manipulating certain dietary components and exercise components. Check out my full video on how I achieved that and what are some of the additional strategies to decrease visceral fat.

=== FILE: What Eating 25% Less Protein Did To My Body [V2Vb6TEC7XU].en.txt ===

=== FILE: What Happens to Your Body If You Stop Eating [SuaOpvMKYG4].en.txt ===

What happens to your body if you stop eating and consuming calories? Within the first 4 to 6 hours, your blood sugar will drop to normal levels since your last meal. The liver breaks down stored glycogen in the liver called glycogen to maintain normal blood sugar for the next 10 to 12 hours. After about 12 hours of not eating, your liver glycogen stores will be low and the body then starts using more fat for energy production. This is characterized by the rise in ketone bodies which are produced from fatty acids. After 24 hours, your body is running on purely body fat by converting body fat into ketone bodies. However, the body still needs some amount of glucose, which is why the liver breaks down amino acids from muscle protein into glucose via a process called gluconioenesis. From 24 hours onward, gluconioenesis rises and reaches its peak at about 3 days of not eating. After 24 hours, you also see an increase in growth hormone, which signals the body to reduce protein breakdown and increase fat burning. After 36 hours, autophagy rises significantly, which is a process of cell cleanup. Autophagy breaks down broken, worn out, and dysfunctional cell components and mitochondria to be used for energy. The longer you don't eat, the more weight you will lose, but this is not always healthy nor sustainable. You will have to eat at some point, and that's why it's important to have a meal plan that you can follow sustainably without needing to crash diet or starve yourself. Try to eat minimally processed foods, practice portion control, and incorporate regular physical activity into your life.

=== FILE: What Lithium Did to My Brain [1JaAVJfcJHM].en.txt ===

I micro doed lithium for two weeks and I'm going to share with you my experience. No, I'm not talking about licking batteries. Here we go. I'm talking about lithium supplements that are often used to improve mood and brain health. Lithium supplements have become quite popular online, which is why I dug up the old research and decided to try it again. I took 5 milligs of lithium oritate every day, and my general experience was that my mood was slightly more elevated. Then I stopped taking lithium to see if I revert back to baseline. Now I don't have any bipolar disorder, mania or depression or anything like that. So I wouldn't be experiencing a massive difference anyway, but those 5 milligs a day were noticeable. I would say my mood was maybe 5% better. And I think my concentration on work was also about 5% better. Of course, this isn't a double blind placeboc controlled randomized control trial. It's just my own subjective experience that has the risk of placebo. However, there is actual clinical research showing that lithium does improve mood and prevent mood episodes prophylactically. Most of that research is done on people with bipolar disorder because lithium has historically been used to treat bipolar disorder. In fact, lithium is the gold standard for treating bipolar disorder and mania. I'm not going to be taking lithium all the time because I don't think I need it.

=== FILE: What Megadosing Creatine Does to Kidneys [cIbRf9t_wX8].en.txt ===

When I mega dosed 28 grams of creatine a day, I noticed improved cognition after sleep deprivation, but not when I was sleeping normally. One of the major comments and concerns people had was, "Isn't it bad for your kidneys, rip kidneys?" And if you're doing something that doesn't require lots of force, then you'll rely mostly on your so-called slow twitch or type one muscle fibers. There's this principle of orderly recruitment that was put forward by Henman decades ago in which the recruitment of motor units increases according to the demands of the task and you start with the slowest twitch fibers and then you move into the intermediate fibers and then you get the highest threshold ones. However, if you're trying to move quickly, then you can recruit all of those different types of fibers from the get- go. And so, if you want to build your power, you can do that provided that you're focusing on moving whatever you're moving quickly. And you might not do that from the start of resistance training program. Let's say that you've not done resistance training before. You're getting accustomed to the new exercises. There are specifics we don't need to get into like the force velocity curve and how training at different intensities can push that around in different directions, but that's only really relevant to athletes. And doing too much work in that type of range could dispose you to injuries. But the intensity needs to be high enough that you are going to get some sort of strength stimulus. You can get roughly equivalent hypertrophy from using intensities as low as about a 20 rep max. So, a weight that you could lift 20 times until you couldn't lift it again with perfect technique. But training at those types of lower intensities isn't going to give you as strong a bone remodeling or strength stimulus. So, just bear that in mind. People often say that athletes are fit, but they don't live longer. That's not true. Studies consistently show that athletes live on average 5 years longer than the general population. But which sport increases life expectancy the most? This 2024 review from 183 countries on up to 100,000 athletes saw that the top five sports for life expectancy were pole vaultting, gymnastics, fencing, targeting sports, racket sports, mixed track and field, race walking, and cricket. The bottom five sports with the shortest life expectancy were sumo wrestling, volleyball, mountaineering, martial arts, and handball. Now, there are some obvious caveats. These athletes were overwhelmingly male, so we don't have data about females. And there may be some other factors such as socioeconomic status that affects these results. However, sumo wrestlers earn almost twice as much money as gymnasts and pole walters, but they still live significantly shorter. So, there can be some element of truth in this study. You do want to do sports, but you don't want to become overweight. And contact sports might have negative effects on your overall lifespan. Another study from Australia found exactly that Olympic athletes lived over three years longer than the general population with the exception of Australian football players and rugby players because of the contact and trauma. So, this new study in science was looking at torine levels across aging in humans, non-human primates, and mice to see if they decline with age. It was previously shown that torine levels decline with age, and that low levels of torine would be harmful to health and longevity. What they found was that circulating torine levels weren't seen to decline with age in humans nor primates. There was actually a lot of individual variability in circulating torine levels, with some people seeing an increase in torine with age, whereas others didn't. For some reason, this has made a lot of people concerned about whether or not torine supplementation is a good idea for healthy aging, thinking that because torine levels were seen to increase with age, it would mean that torine would accelerate biological aging. However, these circulating torine levels had inconsistent health outcomes, which means that there's no consistent relationship between higher torine levels being beneficial nor harmful to health. Aging increases oxidative stress, inflammation, and mitochondrial dysfunction, which could mean the rise in torine is a compensatory physiological response to getting older. Aging also worsens kidney function, and it means the kidneys are less able to excrete torine. Thus, torine accumulates in the blood and tissues. So, elevated torine levels might be a sign of poor kidney function and not causing aging. Women were seen to have higher torine concentrations than men, which might mean there's some sex or weight effects on torine metabolism.
