=== FILE: Why Women Live 5+ Years Longer Than Men [BYzh9QTsCxc].en.txt ===

Women live on average 5 to 10 years longer than men do. Not only that, but centinarians, the people who live over the age of 100, are disproportionarily female. 80 to 90% of them are women. If you look at the list of the oldest people to have ever lived, then the first 27 of them are female. And the first man is number 28. The oldest women were John Clement aged 122 and Kanet Tanaka and Saraknos at age 119. The oldest men were Jerome and Kimura, aged 116, and Christian Mortensson and Emiliano Marcato Del Toro, aged 115. That's a 5-year gap between the oldest living men and the oldest living women, who all have supposedly good genetics and a decent lifestyle that enabled them to live so long. The most obvious explanation for this is that men are unhealthier. They eat worse diets, they drink more alcohol, and they smoke. Men have more dangerous vocations. They follow riskier behavior and they're expected to sacrifice themselves like on the Titanic. But there seems to be something more biological about it as well. You see a similar phenomenon in animals and it's even more skewed. Mamalian females live on average 18.6% longer than mamalian males whereas human females live 7.8% longer than human males. Nobody knows the exact reason why women live longer than men. But there are a few theories. One of the theories is the difference in hormones, especially estrogen and androgens. Women during their reproductive years have on average four times more estrogen than males. Both men and women have estrogen, but women have significantly more. Only after menopause, which happens in women's early 50s, you see a massive drop in estrogen, close to zero. Coincidentally, you see a spike in the risk of hip fractures, heart disease, and Alzheimer's after that. Estrogen is considered the primary female hormone, but it has a lot of other health benefits. Estrogen is cardioprotective, neuroprotective, and it increases the expression of antioxidant enzymes. So, it might be that women have 50 years where their high estrogen levels are slowing down the development of heart disease and neurodeeneration, which means they add an extra 5 to 10 years to their life, whereas men who don't have high estrogen are starting to develop these diseases already in their 30s and 40s. You have to understand that heart disease and Alzheimer's, they don't start in your 50s or 60s. In fact, they start in your youth and they take decades to progress. The higher estrogen levels in women buffer against that progression, which gives them an additional few years of life. Things get really interesting when you see that non-feminizing estrogens like 17 alpha estradiol extend lifespan by 19% in male mice, but not in female mice. Obviously, there are no human trials looking at the effects of 17 alpha estradiol on the effects of heart disease mortality or all cause mortality in humans, but it's quite interesting. In women, hormone replacement therapy with estrogen does appear to reduce the risk of heart disease and all cause mortality, but not for all women of all ages. The optimal time for hormone replacement therapy appears to be in women less than 60 years of age or less than 10 years since menopause. That would support the idea that estrogen reduces the risk of heart disease. Not only is estrogen cardioprotective, but male androgenic hormones appear to be promoting aging. Testosterone is the main androgen, but there's also dehydrotestosterone, DHD, dehydroepi, androsterone, DHEA, androtheenad, and many others. Androgens are responsible for male characteristics such as a deep voice, broad shoulders, higher muscle mass, body hair, etc. As you see from these pictures, you can already know which of these men has high androgens and which one has lower androgens. despite being depicted at the same chronological age with AI. One hypothesis is that androgens have imunosuppressive and pro- clotting effects which could explain the increased risk of heart disease and cancer in men. Men have 10 to 18 times more testosterone in the blood than women and the immunosuppressive effects of testosterone appear to be weaker in women than in men. Androgens like DHT have an immunosuppressive role and they suppress antibbody production and te- cells which can leave the organism more vulnerable to cancer. This might also explain why men have much lower rates of autoimmune diseases than women. Male immune cells are being suppressed by androgens, which does reduce the risk of autoimmunity, but might increase the risk of cancer. Androgen deprivation therapies are one of the main treatment options for prostate cancer that affects only men. It does make the person feel extremely tired and with no libido as well as increase the risk of dementia. But androgen deprivation therapy increases the chance of surviving the cancer, although it doesn't always work. Now, there's no evidence that having normal androgen levels would increase the risk of cancer for an otherwise healthy male, but it appears that high androgen levels when you already have cancer can be harmful. Testosterone obviously is beneficial in many ways, and low testosterone levels are also associated with increased mortality, especially among older men. Low testosterone lowers muscle mass, increases visceral fat mass, and reduces blood sugar regulation, all of which are harmful. So, my takeaway of this research isn't that you should try to lower your testosterone or lower your androgens. It just might be that extremely high androgenic hormones are bad for overall maximum lifespan. I'm talking about living to the age of 120 and beyond. Instead, there are some general health related differences in men and women that can add several years to your life expectancy as a male. When you look at things like body fat percentage and metabolic health, then based on research, men appear to develop cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and metabolic syndrome a lot faster than women do. For women, it's okay to have more body fat, and it doesn't appear to matter how much body fat a woman has, as long as they're not severely underweight or morbidly obese. For men, however, anything above 15% body fat is linearly associated with increased mortality risk and heart disease. The same with fitness. A 2021 UK bioank study found that low card fitness was associated with higher all cause mortality in both men and women, regardless of weight status. However, body fatness modified mortality risk in men but not clearly in women. In men, being obese and unfit significantly raised mortality risk, whereas fit obese men had no elevated risk compared to fit normal weight men. So, as a man, if you want to live longer and you want to reach the age of 100, then you need to be fit and lean rather than fat and unfit. For women, it doesn't appear to matter that much. Women can be slightly overweight and even mildly obese and is not going to increase their mortality risk. And the reason for that might be because of the hormonal differences. Estrogen makes you store more fat around the hips and under your skin, the subcutaneous fat. Whereas men tend to store the body fat more around the organs as visceral fat that is more harmful and increases your risk of heart disease a lot more. Interestingly, anti-diabetic drugs like SGLT2 inhibitors have been seen to extend lifespan in male mice only, but not in female mice, similar to 17 alpha estradiol. In the interventions testing program, one of the SGLT2 inhibitors, Canaglyphloin, was seen to extend median survival of male mice by 14%. And 90th percentile survival by 9%. These mouse studies are done in a controlled environment. The male and female mice are fed the same diets. They're living in the same environment and they're monitored. So, the reason why SGLT2 inhibitors extend lifespan in male mice only might be because of the differences in biology between men and women, perhaps estrogen. So it looks like men are more vulnerable to metabolic diseases and heart disease than women because of differences in hormones. And statistically speaking, if men get heart disease earlier than women do, they will have shorter life expectancy. Now, it doesn't obviously apply to all men. Some men will outlive some women. That's logical. But statistically speaking, men have shorter life expectancy because of increased risk of heart disease that can be caused by a poor lifestyle, some other riskier behaviors, as well as the hormonal differences between men and women as estrogen delays the development of heart disease and neurodeeneration. All right, so let's recap. Men have unhealthier lifestyles and they're more vulnerable to dying because of unhealthy lifestyles and being overweight. The solution, get fit and lean as a man. Secondly, men have lower estrogen and higher androgens, which might drive faster biological aging, but the evidence isn't completely clear. You certainly shouldn't manipulate your hormones in any way based on that. Just focus on being as healthy as you can as a man. That's why I focus on following a healthy lifestyle and staying in optimal health for as long as possible. You can check out my full evidence-based longevity routine video

=== FILE: Why You Need Old Man Strength for Longevity [M8VIzXKm9BI].en.txt ===

Have you ever shaken the hand of an older guy and their grip crushes you? They're otherwise a skinny old man, but they can lift insane amounts of weight with no training. That's old man's strength. And it's more than just a funny phrase. In fact, it could be one of the biggest predictors of how long you're going to live. Research consistently shows that people with higher grip strength, a simple measure of overall upper body strength, have a lower risk of dementia, a lower risk of heart disease, and even a lower risk of dying from all causes. Grip strength is just a measurement of overall body strength. It could be anything. The idea is that people who are generally stronger live longer. I'm talking about the general population, not some sort of a strongman competitor because you can also get stronger while taking steroids. But this is not what we're talking about here. The reason old man's strength is associated with living longer is because muscle mass and strength decline with age. They peak in your mid-30s and late 40s as a man and in your early 40s as a woman. People who maintain more muscle and strength must be doing something right with their physical activity and health, which enables them to maintain more muscle later in life. Having low muscle mass later in life is a predictor of death from all causes. Because with low muscle, you're at a higher risk of diabetes, obesity, Alzheimer's, and falling off the stairs. And when you compare muscle mass and muscle strength, then muscle strength is a stronger predictor of mortality. That's why it's important to think about building old man strength, not old man muscle. The muscle is the byproduct of getting stronger. So, in this video, I'm going to analyze the components of old man's strength. What does it consist of and how you can train it so you too can be a jacked old guy. All right. So, what's old man's strength made of? I would argue it's strong grip and strong forearms, strong back, strong legs and hips, and strong shoulders. Basically, having strong muscles that are developed with functional activities. Old man strength in a colloquial sense is built by physical labor like farming, tossing hay, chopping wood, carrying stones, shoveling, roping fishnetss, reeling in the fishnetss, etc. You don't see a lot of old strong men doing bench presses or biceps curls. Now, it doesn't mean that these exercises wouldn't make you stronger overall, but the strong old men tend to be more formidable in a specific way. They have specifically very big forearms, strong back, and a crushing grip, which is built with specific stimuli that a lot of regular gym workouts tend to miss. If you don't have a physically active job, like construction work or farming, then you have to build your old man's strength with resistance training. There's no other way around it. It's not going to happen in of itself. Let's start with grip strength. I know it's a bit of a meme that grip strength is associated with longevity. Doesn't mean that just training your grip is going to make you live longer. The grip strength is just a way to measure your strength. And people who have higher grip strength are number one, they're stronger and they do things that make you stronger and healthier. It's still quite important to train your grip as it makes you stronger in every other exercise as well. You need to know about the concept of irradiation which describes the principle where contracting one part of your body like your grip is going to make the surrounding muscles also become more tense and stronger. That's why if you grip hard and hold tightly onto something, you're going to be stronger compared to having a loose grip. I'm going to keep it simple. To increase your grip strength, you need to train the squeezing or pinching motion, flexing or rotation motion, and the static hold, where you hold onto something tightly. Whenever you're grabbing or lifting something heavy, you're training all of them, but you can also isolate them specifically. Squeezing can be trained with heavy grip trainers like the Captain Crunch or at the gym, these grip squeezing machines. I don't know what they're called. Pinching can be trained by pinching heavy plates and lifting them off the ground. You can also lift heavy logs or thick bars. The thicker the grip, the harder it is to lift it. Flexing or rotation can be trained by rope climbs, wrist curls, or the grip rotation machines at the gym. Static holds can be trained by dead hangs from a bar. You can add a weighted vest to increase difficulty if you're already quite strong. Farmers carries are also excellent for not only your grip, but also your traps and back. Forearms, reverse curls. Instead of a regular biceps curl that targets primarily your biceps, switch your palms down and do the curls that way. Shoveling. Shoveling or chopping wood is great for forearms. To mimic a shoveling motion at the gym, you can use a weighted bar or a hammer to rotate your forearms. Sandbag or rock lifts. Lifting a sandbag or an odd-shaped object off the ground is harder than lifting barbells or dumbbells, and it forces you to use more of your grip and forearms. Moving on with back exercises. Deadlift is one of the best exercises for old man strength. It trains your grip, forearms, back, hips, and legs to a certain extent. I don't think you necessarily need to deadlift, but if you do, you can expect a lot of gains. Pull-ups, weighted pull-ups are amazing for building a strong back, strong forearms, and strong grip at the same time. Legs and hips. Leg strength is another marker associated with reduced mortality, which makes sense. Stronger legs equals stronger body overall. Squats are one of the best exercises for leg strength. doesn't have to be barbell squats. It can also be goblet squats with a kettle bell, Bulgarian split squats, lunges, etc. They're all great for increasing leg strength. Kettle bell swings are amazing for hip power and mobility. They target the glutes and maintain speed, which also declines with age. Shoulders, shoulder press, some sort of a shoulder pressing is important for everyday living because lifting things over your head is something we all have to do in some shape or form. Shoulder pressing with a barbell, seated dumbbell shoulder press, or even handstand push-ups are all things you can do. kettle bell clean and jerks or snatchers are also quite useful for shoulder strength and mobility. Old strong men do that by lifting hay, lifting logs or something else like that over their head. Lastly, I want to cover the importance of joint health. It's as important to have strong joints as it is to have strong muscles. For strong and healthy joints, you need to focus on quantity of reps rather than intensity. Intensity builds the strength and power, but for joint integrity, you want to direct a lot of blood flow to the joints with good form. Think of doing dozens of bodyweight pull-ups and dips for the elbows and shoulders and dozens of walking lunges and squats for your hips and knees. All of these exercises need to follow what's called progressive overload. This is where a lot of people are confused about the physiology of insulin and how it works. insulin is like a Batman villain in the social media, but the truth is you need insulin to live. Whenever your blood sugar rises because of eating or anything else, your body would produce insulin to shuttle that glucose into cells, and lower the blood sugar down to normal. insulin attaches onto the insulin receptors and lets the glucose in. In type 1 diabetes, insulin is not produced, and blood sugar stays elevated, leading to glycation and other types of tissue damage. In type 2 diabetes, the insulin receptors have become insensitive to insulin, and they're not responding, which also results in high blood sugar levels.
